about: The measure is simplicity: every rule a builder must get right, borrowed or not (DECISIONS V5-1 and V5-6; VERDICT 11.7). The grain is REQUIREMENTS DEV-10 (c): a rule counts when a builder must write it and dropping it, or getting it wrong, breaks a stated property, safety or a stated liveness or performance bar (one guard, one state update, or one comparison that carries correctness). Logging, metrics, config plumbing and speed-only choices are not counted. Anchors are the model counts by ablation: raft-config 16 (E-14b 14 + E-14c 2), healing-self 14, controller-commands 18 and writer-epoch-rlog 9 (E-16), slot moves 28 and split + merge 37 and re-key 36 and fixN 13 on E-17c's real-log footing, the dedup options under fwd (E-20: window 19, sessions 14, producer state 17; keys alone 12), srchi-marks 5 (E-30), writer-time 7 (E-21, simulated), the saga with fenced locks 38 (E-24), restore-mark 8 and genesis 4 and 3 (E-33), subscribe 26 and 27 (E-31), disk-incarnation 2 and par-repair 7 (E-37). Where a model counted rules that belong to another record's state, its total is kept as a bundle: each rule is counted once, in the record that owns the state it guards or writes (the dedup guard with the dedup option, the fence check with fence-tokens, the read rules with subscribe, the move's carry of outcomes with the dedup option), and each bundle's record names where every one of its model's rules went, so the parts still sum to the model count. Records without a model count were counted from a spec or paper read in the pass (basis 'spec'), from source code read in the pass ('code'), or from the design text ('reasoned'; anything about an outside system not checked is marked 'from memory'). low and high bound each count where the grain or the source is uncertain. owner is who writes the code: 'fero', 'library' (imported, such as raft-rs, Go's etcd raft or RocksDB) or 'outside' (another system, such as JetStream for BUY). owner_by_row gives a different owner in named rows (the Raft records in the rows on raft-rs or etcd raft). owner_split splits one record's count by owner. basis_split splits one record's count by basis, where its rules mix bases (the record's basis is then the larger part). row_minus {row: n} names rules of a record that a carrying row does not need (for example a carry rule in a row whose partitions never move, or a rule another record of that row already counts). To sum a row: add each carried key's count, then subtract that key's row_minus for the row. 'BASE' in row_minus means the base row below. issue-order and timeline-merge are recorded but are in no row's list. The base row is the study's MIN row with C self and Z par, changed by V5-2 to V5-5 (see base.decisions).

rules: Only the leader adds new entries to the log.
Each new entry carries the leader's current term.
An append names the index and term of the entry just before its first entry.
A follower refuses an append or a snapshot from an older term.
A follower takes the entries only if it holds an entry at that index with that term.
Where a new entry's term differs from the one held at its index, the follower cuts its log from there.
A follower never cuts entries that match; it adds only the ones it lacks, so a late or repeated append cannot shorten its log.
A replica writes entries to disk before it acks them.
A follower acks the exact index up to which its log now matches the leader's.
After a refused append, the leader steps back and resends from earlier until the logs meet.

High 12 adds 'never cut below the commit index' and 'restart reads back exactly what was fsynced'. Shared: the journal's 'persisted waits for the fdatasync' is the storage side of rule 8; count it once. The term rule for snapshots lives here, not in raft-snapshot.

rules: Term and vote are on disk before any message that depends on them goes out.
A follower or candidate stands when its election timer runs out with no word from a leader; hearing a leader or granting a vote restarts the timer.
Election timeouts have a random part, so two replicas rarely stand at once.
On standing, a replica raises its term by one.
It votes for itself in that term.
It clears its vote tally from earlier terms.
A replica grants a vote only to a request for its own current term.
It grants at most one vote per term: only if it has not voted, or voted for the same candidate.
It grants only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date: a higher last term, or the same last term and at least as long.
A granted vote is recorded as the replica's vote for that term.
A candidate counts a vote reply only if it is for its current term.
A candidate adds each granted vote to its tally.
Only a candidate can become leader; a follower with an old tally never does.
Any message with a higher term makes the receiver take that term.
On a higher term, a leader or candidate steps down to follower.
On a new term, the replica clears its vote.
A candidate that hears from a leader of its own term becomes its follower.

The journal holds terms and votes; rule 1 is the Raft rule, not the journal's.

rules: On winning, the leader resets what it knows each follower holds: its own log end for itself, nothing for the others.
The leader counts an append ack only if it is from its current term.
A success ack raises what the leader knows that follower holds.
The leader counts its own copy only once its own fsync has landed.
The commit index moves to the highest index that a majority of the configuration holds.
The leader commits by counting only an entry of its own term; earlier entries commit with it.
A heartbeat carries a commit index no higher than what that follower is known to hold.
A follower raises its commit index only up to the last entry it knows matches the leader's log.

High 10 adds 'the commit index never goes back' (etcd's commitTo max; likely an equivalent mutant) and the leader-side cap on an append's commit (redundant with rule 8 in etcd's code). The journal's group fsync is the storage side of rule 4; count it once. DESIGN-V5's 'send the commit offset at once on a small ping' is latency only, not counted. CALIBRATED: Rule 5 now says 'a majority of the configuration'. That only voters count is learners' rule 1, so it is not said twice. No count change.

rules: A candidate counts only the votes of its own configuration's voters (r01).
A new leader sets its pending-change mark at its log end, so it waits for older changes (r02).
A new leader first adds an empty entry of its own term (r03, Ongaro's 2015 fix).
Only a leader proposes a membership change (r04).
A leader proposes a change only once its last change is committed (r05).
A leader proposes a change only once it has applied its committed configuration (r06).
A change goes into the log as an entry (r08).
Proposing a change sets the pending-change mark (r09).
A replica applies the latest committed configuration (r17).
A leader that the applied configuration removes steps down (r18).
No member stands while a committed change is still unapplied (r20, the campaign guard).
Only a voter of its own applied configuration stands (r19).
A configuration takes effect when it commits, not when it is appended.
Learners grant votes by the normal log rule.
A lost disk never comes back under its old id.
raft-config.source: E-14 (campaign guard, on commit), E-14b README 'Rules counted' (14: r01-r06, r08, r09, r17, r18, r20, R6, three-ghost, R2-1), E-14c README 'Rules counted' (+2: r19, grow first); TLC on etcd's own TLA+ spec; AMENDMENTS A-01
raft-config.bundle: Membership on commit: E-14b 14 + E-14c 2 = 16 (TLC on etcd's spec). E-14c's 'grow first' is written by the healer (healing-self promote.odd and remove.four; controller-commands c_promote.odd and c_remove.four), and every row with raft-config carries one of the two healers, so it is counted there and raft-config holds 15. Rule 15 is also E-37's ghost rule (disk-incarnation's second rule): it is counted here, because every row with disk-incarnation also carries raft-config, and PD (Z crash, no disk-incarnation) needs it too.
raft-config.rows_note: owner fero on the TS port rows; library on raft-rs or Go's etcd raft rows, except rules 15 and 16, which fero writes in every row (DESIGN-V5 4.1's incarnation; the healing planner). raft-rs rows also add StepDownOnRemoval (rule 10), which raft-rs 0.7.0 lacks (E-10, A-01)
raft-config.notes: Anchor used as given (16). Two of the 16 are counted again by other model counts: rule 15 is E-37's second disk-incarnation rule ('a wiped replica never votes under its old id'; E-37 says E-14's GhostReturn mutant is the same rule), and rule 16 is what E-16's promote.odd and remove.four (healing-self) and c_promote.odd and c_remove.four (controller-commands) enforce. Low 14 is the count once those two are left to disk-incarnation and the healing mechanism; the calibrator should keep each rule in one place. r03 is also Raft's commit-safety rule (a new leader commits an entry of its own term); it is counted here only. CALIBRATED: 16 -> 15. 'Healing grows before it shrinks' left: it is E-16's promote.odd plus remove.four (and their c_ forms), two guards a builder writes in the healer. The ghost rule (15) stays here and leaves disk-incarnation. Low 14 also moves rule 15 out; high 16 counts grow-first here as one rule.

rules: A learner's ack never counts toward a commit.
The leader sends the log to learners as it does to voters.
A learner is promoted only once its log has caught up to the leader's commit offset.

rules: A replica cuts a snapshot only at an index it has applied.
A snapshot records the index and term of its last entry.
A snapshot holds the configuration in force at that index.
A replica writes the snapshot to disk before it drops any log below it.
A replica drops log entries only below its snapshot's index.
The leader sends its snapshot to a replica that needs an entry it has dropped.
A follower ignores a snapshot at or below its commit index.
A follower uses a received snapshot only once all of it has arrived and is on disk.
If the follower's log holds the snapshot's last entry, same index and term, it keeps the entries after it; otherwise it drops its whole log.
The follower resets its fold, its configuration and its commit index from the snapshot.

raft-snapshot.notes: etcd's TLA+ spec models a snapshot only as an append of the whole prefix (SendSnapshot, tla 370), so the count is from the paper's Figure 13 and etcd's restore(), not a model. Overlap: tier's 'drop the log below i only when a reachable snapshot covers i' is rule 5 seen from the object store; count it once (tier keeps only its extra conditions: segment uploaded, no move or fork still reads it). The term check on a snapshot message is raft-log's rule 4. Snapshot layers and the object store are tier's. Low 7 drops the chunk rule (8) and folds 4 into 5; high 11 adds etcd's defence that a snapshot naming a config without the receiver is refused.

rules: Before it raises its term, a replica asks for pre-votes for the next term and changes neither its term nor its vote.
A replica grants a pre-vote by the normal term and log rules, but records no vote and keeps its own term.
A replica refuses a pre-vote or a vote while it has heard from a working leader within the election timeout.
Only with pre-votes from a majority of voters does a replica raise its term and stand.
A leader notes each voter it hears from in the current check period.
A leader that has not heard from a majority of voters within an election timeout steps down.
On a quiet group, a voter counts as heard while its link pings answer.

The transfer exception to rule 3 is raft-leader-transfer's. Low 5 folds rule 3 into rule 2 and rule 7 into link-pings; high 9 adds etcd's 'a rejected pre-vote with a higher term makes the asker take that term' and clearing the check marks each period.

rules: While a transfer runs, the leader takes no new writes.
Writes that arrive during the transfer are refused with the target's name, never dropped or held.
The leader sends TimeoutNow only once the target holds its whole log.
On TimeoutNow, the target stands at once, skipping its timer and PreVote, and marks its vote requests as a transfer.
Voters grant a transfer's vote request even while they still hear from the old leader.
If the transfer has not finished within an election timeout, the leader gives it up and takes writes again.

High 7 adds etcd's 'transfer only to a voter, never a learner' (raft.go 1629), which a checker would likely call equivalent, since a learner cannot stand (raft-config r19) and rule 6 ends the attempt. rules: A leader serves a read index only after it has committed an entry of its own term; until then reads wait.
It takes its current commit index as the read's index.
It confirms it still leads with one round in its own term, matched to the read and acked by a majority of voters; a link ping never counts.
It answers only once its fold has reached the read's index.
raft-readindex.source: Raft thesis 6.4; etcd raft v3.7.0-rc (commit c51f010), tla/etcdraft.tla and raft.go, read in the Go module cache: raft.go 1357 and 2122-2125 (no read index before an entry of the leader's term commits), read_only.go (acks matched to the read's context); DESIGN-V5 4.2 'Reads' and 4.5 read(fresh); E-46 (linearizable in every Maelstrom run)

rules: Two members that share a group send a ping every ping.ms when no other frame went that way.
Any frame from a peer counts as a sign of life, not only a ping.
A peer silent past evict.after is gone to this member.
The gone mark clears as soon as the peer answers again.
link-pings.source: DESIGN-V5 4.2 'Failure detection' (ping every ping.ms when no other frame went that way; gone past evict.after); SPACE 2 C; AMENDMENTS A-12; CockroachDB store liveness (from memory)
link-pings.rows_note: the same in every row that has it; the peer bound past 100 members (A-12) is not counted
link-pings.notes: Not counted here: clocks riding the pings (writer-time), CheckQuorum on a quiet group (raft-prevote-checkquorum rule 7), a quiet follower waking when the leader's link goes silent (quiet-groups rule 6), #meta's cluster-wide gone mark (meta-members). E-16 treated gone marks as world steps, so no model counts these. A-12's bound on linked peers past 100 members is a cost rule (n squared frames), not correctness.

rules: A leader goes quiet only when no write, read or change is in flight and none came for two ticks.
A leader goes quiet only once every live voter holds its commit offset.
It sends 'quiet at i' and then stops sending for that group.
A follower told 'quiet at i' stops its election timer only if it holds i; if it is below i, it asks the leader to wake.
Any write or read index wakes the group before it is handled.
A quiet follower whose link to the leader goes silent for election.ms wakes the group and may stand.
When a link comes back, each side reports its log ends for the groups they share, and the leader wakes any group whose follower is behind.
quiet-groups.source: DESIGN-V5 4.2 'Quiet shards' and the failure-detection table ('a quiet shard's leader dies'); AMENDMENTS A-12; CockroachDB quiesced ranges and its lagging-follower rule (from memory); E-11, E-25 (measured, no failure injected)
quiet-groups.rows_note: fero writes it in every row; etcd raft and raft-rs have no quiescence (TiKV's hibernate regions live in TiKV, from memory)
quiet-groups.notes: Never modelled with failures (E-11 and E-25 measured idle cost only). 'Two ticks' is a constant. Rule 5 is also the catalogue's readindex wake; counted here only. Low 5 merges 1 with 2 and 3 with 4; high 8 splits rule 4 into its guard and its wake request.

rules: Only a quiet, fully committed group goes dormant.
Its record of term, vote, commit and log end is on disk before the group leaves memory.
A message, write or open for a dormant group loads its record before anything is handled; nothing answers for it from an empty default.
The member that wakes a group for a write stands at once, so the write is not held for an election timeout.
dormant-groups.source: AMENDMENTS A-15; E-26 README (sleep: a quiet, fully committed group written as a 24-byte record with one fdatasync; wake: read the record and campaign at once, a follower on the first message); E-36; TiKV hibernate regions (from memory)
dormant-groups.rows_note: only rows with G shard that price A-15; not MIN-P or the pslot rows, not OBJ
dormant-groups.notes: Rule 4 carries DEP-04 (writable within 1.5 s of a wake, below election.ms). Low 3 drops it as a timing rule. High 5 adds 'the dormant record is rewritten whenever term or vote change while asleep', which rule 3 makes impossible (any message wakes it first).

rules: Each member reports its step and fsync latency, and the controller keeps a score per member over a window.
The controller moves leaderships off a member whose score stays k times its peers', to a caught-up voter on a faster member.
A member moved off for slowness is no transfer target or preferred leader until its score has been normal for a hold time.
slow-leader-controller.source: AMENDMENTS A-03; E-38 README F-18 finding (a leader whose step or fsync latency stays above k times its peers' hands over; PD's evict-slow-store scheduler, from memory); REQUIREMENTS F-18 (MUST)
slow-leader-controller.rows_note: rows with C cent or cent-co; the transfer itself is raft-leader-transfer's, and a command's epoch check and timeout are controller-commands'
slow-leader-controller.notes: Named, never built or modelled (A-03). It carries F-18 (a 10 times slower leader gives up within 5 E). Rule 3 stops flapping against healing's settle.ms hand-back (DEV-02). High 5 adds a re-check where the command runs and a timeout for a failed transfer, if they are not taken from controller-commands.

rules: Each leader keeps a latency score for itself and for each follower over a window.
A leader whose score stays k times its followers' hands leadership to its most caught-up fast follower.
A member that handed off for slowness takes no leadership back, and is no preferred leader, until its score has been normal for a hold time.
slow-leader-self.source: AMENDMENTS A-03; E-38 README F-18 finding ('a leader whose own step or fsync latency stays above k times its followers' for a window hands leadership to its most caught-up follower'); REQUIREMENTS F-18 (MUST)
slow-leader-self.rows_note: rows with C self or self+p; no precedent on offer for this form
slow-leader-self.notes: Named, never built or modelled. Same shape as slow-leader-controller: the decider is the leader itself, so no command or epoch check is needed. A leader judging itself while slow is a doubt (reasoned). Rule 3 must also hold back healing's settle.ms hand-back to the preferred leader, or the two undo each other.

A leaving member marks itself retiring before anything else.

rules: The first open that creates a resource writes its record, with its first group and slots, only if no record exists.
A later open whose options differ is refused, naming the difference, unless an alter in progress allows its code hash.
An alter changes the record online, and a roll adds the new code hash before it removes the old one.
A server becomes a full replica of a resource's group only if it can run one of the resource's allowed code hashes.
The seed is applied only once, and the record marks it applied in the same step.
While the write gate is read-only, every write is refused with its reason.
meta-catalog.source: DESIGN-V5 4.2 '#meta' resource record; 4.5 'Defining and changing a resource' (first open writes the catalog; a differing open is refused unless an alter allows its hash; alter rolls hashes; a full replica needs the resource's hashes)
meta-catalog.rows_note: rows with a metadata group. Under V5-2 the same rules hold for a resource's settings record in its own log
meta-catalog.notes: Not modelled. Rule 1 is a per-resource conditional create, not the cluster's (genesis-conditional-create). The fold version (fold-version) and cluster version are apart. Low 4 if the gate and the seed mark are folded into the write path; high 7 adds the check of an alter's keys against each other.

rules: After each config change, a group's leader rewrites the group's record.
A record names the config it describes, and an older config never overwrites a newer one.
An operator recovery raises the group's incarnation in its record.
A leader that sees a higher incarnation for its own group stops leading.
A removed replica deletes its copy only once the record shows the group's config without it.
A group's record is deleted only after the slot table has shown none of its slots for settle.ms.
A group's record is deleted only once its history is safe.
After #meta is rebuilt, every group leader writes its record again.
meta-directory.source: DESIGN-V5 4.2 '#meta' shard record ('a hint ... the newest config winning'), 'A removed replica', 'Mixed versions, recovery and routing' (recover --unclean bumps the incarnation; the residual case; recover --new-cluster re-writes)
meta-directory.rows_note: rows with a metadata group. Under V5-3 the directory is soft announcements with no log: rules 1, 2 and 5 stay in the announcement form, rules 3, 4 and 8 move to each resource's own log or go
meta-directory.notes: Not modelled. The slot table's own writes (target writes before it opens, recovery writes at the new epoch) are slot-table's; the epoch high-water mark is restore-mark's. Low 5 counts only the routing-hint rules (1, 2, 5, 6, 7) and leaves recovery rules (3, 4, 8) to the operator-recovery path.

A leader whose own link to a member's life is up ignores a gone hint for it.
A leader adds or promotes a member a hint names only while its own links reach that member.
A lead hint also sets the group's preferred leader, so the settle.ms hand-back does not undo it.
Leaders hand over every group a drained member leads, and a drained member is no preferred leader.

rules: A log replica votes and keeps the log, but never folds rows or serves clients.
It keeps every entry that no snapshot in the object store covers yet.
It stands only when no full voter has won an election for twice election.ms.
While it leads, it takes no client write and refuses with no-writer.
While it leads and a full voter is live, it brings that voter up to its log end and hands it leadership.
With no full voter live, it adds a full replica as a learner, loaded from the object store's snapshot and its own tail, promotes it, then hands it leadership; with no object store it waits.
Healing places log replicas only when a group has fewer server candidates than copies.

project-groups.rows_note: rows with G pslot (MIN-P and its hybrids, COMP, COMP2)

write.pos: a record's position is (lane, log index).
write.append: the writer appends the write and answers it once it commits.
refuse.answer: the writer sends the refusal answer.
lanes.source: E-17 fixN ablation (experiments/E17-partitioning/results/fixN-ablation.json: 13 kept of 14); E-17c section 5 C count: fixN stays 13 in a real log and on the bigger bounds (experiments/E17c-partitioning-rerun/README.md)

rules: write.open: a group takes a write only for a slot its committed log holds open; otherwise it answers moved or wrong-shard.
write.append: the writer appends the write and answers it once it commits.
refuse.answer: the writer sends the refusal answer.
slot-table.source: E-17 part 1 slot ablation (experiments/E17-partitioning/results/slot-ablation.json, 26 kept of 69) and E-17c section 5 C count 28 (experiments/E17c-partitioning-rerun/README.md); DESIGN-V5.md 4.2 'The slot table'
slot-table.bundle: Slot moves on E-17c's real-log footing (the C count): 28, crash-only, no give-up, counting fixN's 13 base rules. Own rules: slot-table 3 + slot-sequence 2 + slot-move 13 = 18. The other 10 are counted once, in the mechanism that owns their state, which every slot row carries: write.dedup and refuse.dedup in the row's dedup option (apply.notin, refuse_r.notin); write.fence in fence-tokens (step.fence); refuse.stale in writer-judging rule 2 (a refusal waits for the commit, A-04); read.committed, read.after, read.next, read.take and read.cursor in subscribe (rec.committed, gotrec.is, gotrec.apply, gotrec.cursor: E-31 checks 'after' and 'next' as one comparison); final.outs in the dedup option's carry (fence.outs). move-policy is outside the model (0 of the 28) and adds its own 3. pslot moves need the same 28 (E-17c, probe slotkey).
slot-table.rows_note: Every slot row (DRAFT, MIN, RUST, SRV, LEAN, SLOG, OBJ, MIN-P, MIN-TS, RLOG, EMB-V8, SIDE, COMP, the COMP2 and MIN-P+par hybrids, BASE).
slot-table.notes: The bundle's total is model-checked; the split across members is judgement. slot-table gets the route guard plus 11 of fixN's 13 base write-path rules (the same base lanes counts as 13); the stamp (write.pos) goes to slot-sequence. In E-17's model a group knows it holds a slot from its own log, so the #meta table is only a routing hint and none of its own rules is in the 28. High 16 adds E-15's table rules, needed once a table write can lag or be undone: the target writes s to B before it opens; after an abort it writes s back to A before A reopens; a recovery writes the row at the slot's new epoch; the table keeps the highest version of each row (E-15, DESIGN-V5 4.2). Under V5-2 the table is records in the resource's own log, which does not remove those rules if the table and the slot's data group are different groups. Shared rules counted elsewhere too: write.dedup and refuse.dedup are the same guards as the dedup option's apply.notin and refuse_r.notin (client-sessions, dedup-window, producer-state, caller-keys); write.fence and refuse.stale are the fence-tokens guard and writer-time's pwrite.fence; the five read.* rules are subscribe's cursor rules (E-31); write.append and refuse.answer are the answer half of writer-judging. Count each once. Also: ISR (P fixN) and V4 (P ring) carry no P mechanism from this batch, so they pay none of these base rules while every slot, split, lane and re-key row does; either add fixN's 13 to ISR (and v4's own write path to V4) or take the base out of every P bundle. CALIBRATED: 12 -> 3. Shared with other models, counted once in their home: write.dedup and refuse.dedup (the dedup option's apply.notin and refuse_r.notin; in the PD rows two-phase-commit's own txn-id rules), write.fence (fence-tokens step.fence; in the PD rows two-phase-commit's conflict checks), refuse.stale (writer-judging rule 2), the five read rules (subscribe's rec.committed, gotrec.is, gotrec.apply, gotrec.cursor). What stays is the slot's own guard (write.open) and the two answer rules of the write path, which no other record counts. High 7 adds E-15's four table rules (needed once the table can lag behind an open: unclean recovery, abort).

slot-move.source: E-17 part 1 slot ablation (experiments/E17-partitioning/results/slot-ablation.json) plus E-17c sections 5 R and C (experiments/E17c-partitioning-rerun/README.md); AMENDMENTS A-17
slot-move.bundle: Slot moves on E-17c's real-log footing (the C count): 28, crash-only, no give-up, counting fixN's 13 base rules. Own rules: slot-table 3 + slot-sequence 2 + slot-move 13 = 18. The other 10 are counted once, in the mechanism that owns their state, which every slot row carries: write.dedup and refuse.dedup in the row's dedup option (apply.notin, refuse_r.notin); write.fence in fence-tokens (step.fence); refuse.stale in writer-judging rule 2 (a refusal waits for the commit, A-04); read.committed, read.after, read.next, read.take and read.cursor in subscribe (rec.committed, gotrec.is, gotrec.apply, gotrec.cursor: E-31 checks 'after' and 'next' as one comparison); final.outs in the dedup option's carry (fence.outs). move-policy is outside the model (0 of the 28) and adds its own 3. pslot moves need the same 28 (E-17c, probe slotkey).
slot-move.rows_note: Every slot row. In pslot rows (MIN-P, COMP, the hybrids) the same 14: E-17c's slotkey probe shows pslot needs no more rules than slot on the same footing.
slot-move.notes: Low 12 is the shared sweep (part 1's 26 less the two once guards). High 22 adds a one-decider give-up path: slot+abort is 33 to 34 on the shared footing, so 7 to 8 more rules (B's importing and abort entries, give up or finish never both, hand back only on a committed abort, A reopens only a move it fenced), plus the 2 once guards. E-15's footing (unclean recovery, cancel, abort, table in #meta) counts the move at 31 with no reads; the two footings are not compared (A-17). The carried set's other parts are counted with their own mechanisms: srchi marks (srchi-marks fence.carry/open.carry), segment names (subscribe, E-31: 27), the new epoch in the restore mark (restore-mark, E-33). Overlap: final.outs is the same carry as the dedup option's fence.outs/open.outs (and fence.floor/open.floor, fence.hi/open.hi in E-20); final.tok is the fence-tokens carry if that count includes one. Count each once. CALIBRATED: 14 -> 13. final.outs is the dedup option's carry (fence.outs/open.outs in E-20), counted there. final.recs is also E-31's bopen.fold and fold-all's old rule 5; counted here only. Low 11: the shared sweep less the two once guards and final.outs. High 21 adds the one-decider give-up path (7 to 8 rules).

rules: Move a slot from the busiest group to the least loaded, choosing the slot nearest half the gap; the draft's halving alone leaves groups 1.5 to 2 times uneven (SC-03).
Make a move only when it lowers the busier of the two groups by a margin; without it two equal pieces swap back and forth for ever (SC-04, no flapping).
Shrink a group only after it has been quiet for shrink.after, and only when the group taking its slots stays under half the limits, so a shrink never sets off a grow (SC-04).
move-policy.source: E-18 (experiments/E18-slot-balance/README.md: the controller, the margin trap in 48 of 300 cases, halving fails); AMENDMENTS A-18; DESIGN-V5.md 4.2 'The shard rule'; REQUIREMENTS SC-03, SC-04
move-policy.bundle: Outside E-17c's 28: the move model has no policy, so move-policy's share of the 28 is 0. Its 3 rules come from E-18 and the design. Slot moves on E-17c's real-log footing (the C count): 28, crash-only, no give-up, counting fixN's 13 base rules.
move-policy.rows_note: Every slot row. Under V5-2 each resource's leader runs it; in cent and cent-co rows the controller does, with the same rules.
move-policy.notes: Not in any ablation model. A-18 calls it a load policy with no safety rule (0 by DEV-10 (a)'s letter), which is the low bound. The owner's grain counts a rule whose loss breaks a stated property: SC-04 says no flapping and E-18 simulated the endless swap without the margin, and E-18 showed the halving rule fails SC-03's balance. Rule 3 is from DESIGN-V5's shard rule and SC-04's 'one grow and one shrink a day', not simulated. 'One move at a time' is not needed for safety (E-17c: not even with a third group) and is left out; high 5 adds it (a lease per resource) and E-18's act-and-stop marks (1.25 and 1.10). Treated the same way as split-policy.

write.nofrz: an old cell takes no write once its freeze is in its log.

read.gen: a cell refuses a cursor of another generation (unknown-log).

start.src: a re-key copies from the current generation.
start.append: the catalog logs the re-key's start.
cut.append: the catalog logs the cut-over.

final.frzcom: the final copy covers the old cell's committed freeze.

final.tok: the final copy carries the highest lock token.

final.append: the new cell logs the final copy.
final.once: a new cell takes the final copy from each source only once (needed in a real log, E-17c).

flip.append: the catalog logs the flip.
rekey.source: E-17 rekey ablation (experiments/E17-partitioning/results/rekey-ablation.json: 35 kept of 57) and E-17c sections 5 R and C (experiments/E17c-partitioning-rerun/README.md: 36 to 38 as CELL writes it); experiments/E17-partitioning/options/rekey/README.md
rekey.bundle: Re-key on E-17c's real-log footing: 36 (35 as written + final.once) = rekey 24 + 12 counted in their homes: write.dedup and refuse.dedup (the dedup option's apply.notin and refuse_r.notin; in the PD rows two-phase-commit's own txn-id rules), write.fence (fence-tokens step.fence; in the PD rows two-phase-commit's conflict checks), refuse.stale (writer-judging rule 2), the five read rules (subscribe's rec.committed, gotrec.is, gotrec.apply, gotrec.cursor). Before calibration, low 29 was rekey-carry on the shared sweep. A give-up path (abandon) would add 5 to 6 (E-17 rekey README). Re-key fails SC-08(b) and (f) by design (E-17c, model-checked); that is a property loss, not a rule count. 13 of the 36 are fixN's base write path (write.route, write.pos and the 11 base rules). Shared rules counted elsewhere too: write.dedup and refuse.dedup are the same guards as the dedup option's apply.notin and refuse_r.notin (client-sessions, dedup-window, producer-state, caller-keys); write.fence and refuse.stale are the fence-tokens guard and writer-time's pwrite.fence; the five read.* rules are subscribe's cursor rules (E-31); write.append and refuse.answer are the answer half of writer-judging. Count each once. Also: ISR (P fixN) and V4 (P ring) carry no P mechanism from this batch, so they pay none of these base rules while every slot, split, lane and re-key row does; either add fixN's 13 to ISR (and v4's own write path to V4) or take the base out of every P bundle. CALIBRATED: 36 -> 24. Besides the 9 base rules and final.outs, restart.take and restart.cursor are the same as subscribe's gotsnap rules, which CELL carries. Low 19: rekey-carry (29) on the shared sweep less the same 10 homes. High 26 adds freeze.once and flip.once (undecided at 1.5 million states).

rules: write.nosplit: the parent takes no write to the split-off part once the split entry is in its log.
split.open: a group splits only a partition it holds (needed once a third group exists, E-17c).
split.append: the parent logs the split entry, which is the decision and the fence in one.
init.splcom: the child starts only from the parent's committed split.
init.rows: the child's start entry carries the rows at the split.
init.tok: the child's start entry carries the highest lock token.
init.append: the child logs its start entry.
init.once: the child starts only once (needed in a real log, E-17c).

split-record.bundle: Split + merge on E-17c's real-log footing: 37 = range-table 3 + split-record 8 + merge-record 11 + lineage 4 = 26 own, + 11 in their homes: write.dedup and refuse.dedup (the dedup option's apply.notin and refuse_r.notin; in the PD rows two-phase-commit's own txn-id rules), write.fence (fence-tokens step.fence; in the PD rows two-phase-commit's conflict checks), refuse.stale (writer-judging rule 2), the five read rules (subscribe's rec.committed, gotrec.is, gotrec.apply, gotrec.cursor). And init.outs and merged.outs (the dedup option's carry). split-policy is outside the model and adds its own 3. The PD rows carry no lineage and no fence table: there the bundle is 22 own (range-table, split-record, merge-record) less init.tok and merged.tok (row_minus).
split-record.rows_note: SPLIT and the PD family (PD, PD+fix, TiKV-TS, TiKV-persisted).
split-record.notes: E-17b's '9-rule split' includes the lineage base (init.base) and read.lin; here those two go to lineage and the two E-17c rules (split.open, init.once) come in, so the split itself is still 9. Low 7 is the shared sweep without them. A split has no give-up path (one entry; a crash before commit just loses it). High 10 adds a reasoned rule for prefix or user partitions: never split inside one partition (the partition is the unit of order). Overlap: init.outs and init.tok are the dedup and fence-token carries, as in slot-move. CALIBRATED: 9 -> 8. init.outs is the dedup option's carry, counted there. row_minus: the PD rows keep no fence table (their fence is two-phase-commit's conflict check), so init.tok is not needed there.

rules: write.nosub: the group being removed takes no write once its subsumed entry is in its log.
merge.append: the surviving group logs the merging entry.
subsume.mrgcom: the group being removed freezes only for the survivor's committed merging entry.
subsume.open: it freezes only a partition its committed log holds.
subsume.append: it logs the subsumed entry.
merged.subcom: the survivor takes the partition only from a committed subsumed entry.
merged.rows: the merged entry carries the rows at the freeze.
merged.tok: the merged entry carries the highest lock token.
merged.gen: the merged range gets a new generation, the higher of both sides plus one.
merged.append: the survivor logs the merged entry.
merged.once: the survivor takes a merge only once (needed in a real log, E-17c).

merge-record.notes: E-17b's 11-rule merge plus E-17c's once guard. Low 11 is the shared sweep. rules: write.open: a group takes a write only for a partition its committed log holds; otherwise it answers moved or wrong-shard.
write.append: the writer appends the write and answers it once it commits.
refuse.answer: the writer sends the refusal answer.

range-table.notes: Like slot-table: the route guard plus 11 of fixN's base write-path rules. The range's generation is written by merged.gen (merge-record), and the 'refuse a command made on an older generation' check is what write.nosplit and write.nosub do in the model. High 14 adds two reasoned rules a real router needs: a route or command made on an older generation is refused and refreshed (TiKV's region epoch check), and the table keeps only the highest generation of each range. Shared rules counted elsewhere too: write.dedup and refuse.dedup are the same guards as the dedup option's apply.notin and refuse_r.notin (client-sessions, dedup-window, producer-state, caller-keys); write.fence and refuse.stale are the fence-tokens guard and writer-time's pwrite.fence; the five read.* rules are subscribe's cursor rules (E-31); write.append and refuse.answer are the answer half of writer-judging. Count each once. Also: ISR (P fixN) and V4 (P ring) carry no P mechanism from this batch, so they pay none of these base rules while every slot, split, lane and re-key row does; either add fixN's 13 to ISR (and v4's own write path to V4) or take the base out of every P bundle. CALIBRATED: 12 -> 3. Shared with other models, counted once in their home: write.dedup and refuse.dedup (the dedup option's apply.notin and refuse_r.notin; in the PD rows two-phase-commit's own txn-id rules), write.fence (fence-tokens step.fence; in the PD rows two-phase-commit's conflict checks), refuse.stale (writer-judging rule 2), the five read rules (subscribe's rec.committed, gotrec.is, gotrec.apply, gotrec.cursor). High 5 adds the two reasoned router rules (refuse a command made on an older generation; keep the highest generation of each range).

rules: Split a range at the point that evens its measured load between the two halves (SC-03).
Merge a range only after it has stayed under the merge limits for a quiet period since its last split; otherwise it splits and merges back and forth (SC-04, no flapping).
Merge only when the merged range stays well under the split limits, so a merge never sets off a split (SC-04).
split-policy.source: DESIGN-V5 decision 20a; AMENDMENTS A-18 (a load policy is counted the same wherever it lives); REQUIREMENTS SC-03, SC-04; TiKV's split-merge interval and load-based split (from memory)
split-policy.bundle: Outside E-17c's 37 (the model has no policy); counted on its own, as move-policy is.
split-policy.rows_note: SPLIT (each leader decides) and the PD family (the controller's schedulers decide).
split-policy.notes: Counted on the same terms as move-policy: 0 by A-18's letter (low), and by the owner's grain one rule per guard whose loss breaks SC-03 or SC-04. Not simulated: E-18 did not run splits. 'Split only a range it holds' is split-record's split.open, not here. High 4 adds, for PD, that the controller never schedules a split and a merge on the same range at once (from memory).

rules: write.pos: the writer stamps each record with the slot's next sequence, read from the log end.
final.seq: the final copy carries the slot's sequence, so the target goes on from it and never goes back.
slot-sequence.source: E-17 part 1 slot ablation (experiments/E17-partitioning/results/slot-ablation.json: write.pos and final.seq, both break P2) and E-17c (experiments/E17c-partitioning-rerun/README.md); DESIGN-V5.md 4.3 'The record'
slot-sequence.bundle: Slot moves on E-17c's real-log footing (the C count): 28, crash-only, no give-up, counting fixN's 13 base rules. Own rules: slot-table 3 + slot-sequence 2 + slot-move 13 = 18. The other 10 are counted once, in the mechanism that owns their state, which every slot row carries: write.dedup and refuse.dedup in the row's dedup option (apply.notin, refuse_r.notin); write.fence in fence-tokens (step.fence); refuse.stale in writer-judging rule 2 (a refusal waits for the commit, A-04); read.committed, read.after, read.next, read.take and read.cursor in subscribe (rec.committed, gotrec.is, gotrec.apply, gotrec.cursor: E-31 checks 'after' and 'next' as one comparison); final.outs in the dedup option's carry (fence.outs). move-policy is outside the model (0 of the 28) and adds its own 3. pslot moves need the same 28 (E-17c, probe slotkey).
slot-sequence.notes: The catalogue's 'one rule carries the sequence' is final.seq; the stamp itself is write.pos. High 3 adds the epoch rule outside the crash-only footing: after an unclean recovery or an abort the slot reopens in a new epoch, so no position names two records (E-15, DESIGN-V5 4.2). Recording each new epoch in the restore mark first is restore-mark's (E-33), not here. CALIBRATED: No count change. write.pos is also restore-mark's write.seq and lock.seq (a lock grant is a write); counted here only.

rules: write.pos: a record's position is (generation, group, log index).
read.lin: a reader reads a record after a start or merged entry only once its cursor has reached that entry's base.
init.base: the child's start entry records the partition's last position in the parent (its base).
merged.base: the merged entry records a base too, so a reader can cross a merge (bigger bound, E-17b and E-17c).
lineage.source: E-17b split ablation (experiments/E17-partitioning/results/split-ablation.json: write.pos, read.lin, init.base) and E-17b/E-17c readback bound (merged.base, P4 in 15 steps)

lineage.rows_note: SPLIT only (O off+lin). The PD family uses timestamp positions (closed-timestamps) and carries no lineage.
lineage.notes: The catalogue counts 2 lineage rules on the shared bounds and 3 with a reader across a merge; here the position stamp write.pos is added, because each row's stamp goes to its position mechanism (slot-sequence for slot rows); it belongs to lineage and not range-table so that PD, which has no lineage, does not pay it twice. Low 3 is the shared sweep (no merged.base). High 5 adds a retention rule: a base is kept for ever, or at least while any reader may hold a cursor from before it (SPACE 2 O off+lin says 'kept for ever').

rules: Closing time T is a promise: no write at or below T commits after the log position the close names.
Track each write from when its timestamp is chosen until it has a log position, and never close at or above a tracked write.
Push every new write's timestamp above the closed timestamp before it is proposed.
A tracked write that never reaches the log is retried until the named position has passed, or the leader stops serving.
Publish each closed timestamp together with the log position a follower must apply first.
A follower serves a read or a feed at T only when T is at or below the closed timestamp and it has applied that position.
A new leader or lease starts above the last closed timestamp, so no one writes at or below it after a handover.
A merge carries the removed group's closed timestamp, and the survivor never writes or closes below it.
A change feed's resolved time stays below the oldest unresolved lock; time T is emitted only once every lock below T is resolved.
closed-timestamps.source: CockroachDB RFC 'Follower Reads' (docs/RFCS/20180603_follower_reads.md, read this pass at raw.githubusercontent.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/master): closing promise, proposal tracker, retry or exit, forwarding, MLAI, follower checks, lease transfer, Subsume on merge, intents for CDC; TiKV resolved ts (from memory)
closed-timestamps.rows_note: The PD family (PD, PD+fix, TiKV-TS, TiKV-persisted), which take O hlc.
closed-timestamps.notes: Counted at the models' grain from the RFC's own rule list. Low 7 is the newer shape where the closed timestamp rides in the Raft log itself (CockroachDB's v2, from memory): the separate position check and the retry-or-exit rule fold into log order. High 11 is the RFC's side-transport shape: plus a closed timestamp is kept per lease epoch and dropped when the epoch changes, and a gap in updates resets a follower's state. A split needs nothing (both sides share a leader). The record's position is its commit timestamp, stamped by the two-phase commit; that stamp is counted with 2pc and txn, not here. Writer time for TTLs comes from timestamp-oracle in these rows.

rules: Judge dedup, shape checks, rules and conditions against the log-end state: the committed state plus the writer's uncommitted tail.
Send a refusal, an empty claim or a call-diverged answer only once the log end it was judged on has committed (A-04).
A writer deposed before its entry commits answers unknown, never applied or refused.
Append only results: followers, readers and replays apply plain values and never re-run a check, an op or a rule.
A new leader folds its whole log, earlier terms' uncommitted entries included, before it judges anything.
A batch to one partition is judged as one: all of it is appended, or none.
writer-judging.source: DESIGN-V5.md 4.3 'At the writer', 'Refusals', 'Appending results', 'Two states on the writer'; AMENDMENTS A-04; E-22 F1 (a phantom conflict in 10 of 100 seeds without the commit wait, measured) and E-22b
writer-judging.notes: A-04 priced this at 2 rules (the low bound), counting only what E-22 found missing. The other four are in the design text and each guards a stated property (P-14 linearizable per partition, DATA-01 the same fold on every copy), but none was ablated. Left out because counted elsewhere: 'only for a slot this group holds open' (slot-table and range-table write.open); 'dedup first' (the dedup option's refuse_r.notin); the success answer after commit (the base write.append). High 9 adds: checks run in a fixed order (shape, rules, conditions, then ops); every computed value is checked for encoding and size before it is appended; and A-04's second rule, a session-bound write is sent only after its session record commits (E-22 F2), which belongs to whatever mechanism owns session-bound rows (the #sessions leases), not to dedup.

rules: send.window: the issuer keeps its open call ids within the window W.
resend.horizon: the issuer stops retrying an attempt R after its first send.
giveup.late: after R the attempt ends unknown.
recv.latest: the issuer accepts only the answer to its latest copy.
forward.age: a relay takes the time it held a copy off the copy's budget.
forward.once: a relay forwards a copy only once, over the link it had.
restart.life: a restarted process takes a new issuer id.
apply.notin: apply an attempt only if it is not among the outcomes at the log end.
apply.floor: apply it only above the floor (the highest id minus the window).
apply.budget: apply it only while the copy's budget is not spent.
refuse_r.notin: refuse a resent attempt only if it is not among the outcomes.
refuse_r.budget: refuse a resent attempt only while its budget is not spent.
refuse_f.first: a refusal is left out of the log only for a first send.
stale.floor: an attempt at or below the floor is answered stale-attempt.
forget.silent: forget an issuer only after it has been silent for the horizon.
fence.outs: a slot's fence carries the slot's outcomes.
fence.hi: the fence carries each issuer's highest id.
open.outs: the open takes the carried outcomes.
open.hi: the open takes the carried highest ids, merged by max.
dedup-window.rows_note: DRAFT, LANE, SPLIT, SLOG, V4. Every one also carries route-forward, so the fwd count 19 applies; 17 on a path with no relay.
dedup-window.notes: The two hop rules (forward.age, forward.once) are counted here, not in route-forward, as the catalogue says. Overlap: apply.notin and refuse_r.notin are the base write path's write.dedup and refuse.dedup (in slot-table, range-table, lanes, rekey); fence.outs/open.outs are slot-move's final.outs (and split's init.outs, merged.outs). High 20 adds DESIGN-V5 4.3's 'a leader closes a link that misses pings for election.ms, so a frozen server's late forward never lands', which the model's one global clock cannot show. CALIBRATED: No count change. This record is now the one home of the dedup guard that E-17's base write path also wrote (write.dedup, refuse.dedup), and of the moves' carry of outcomes (E-17's final.outs, init.outs, merged.outs; rekey's final.outs). CALIBRATED: row_minus LANE 4: LANE never moves a partition, so fence.outs, fence.hi, open.outs and open.hi are not needed there.

rules: recv.latest: the client accepts only the answer to its latest copy.
restart.life: a restarted process takes a new session.
apply.notin: apply an attempt only if it is not among the session's outcomes at the log end.
apply.floor: apply it only at or above the session's floor (the client's lowest unacknowledged id, sent with every copy).
apply.live: apply it only while the session has not expired in the registry (committed).
refuse_r.notin: refuse a resent attempt only if it is not among the session's outcomes.
refuse_f.first: a refusal is left out of the log only for a first send.
stale.floor: a copy below the session's floor is answered stale.
expired.dead: answer unknown only once the session's expiry has committed in the registry.
fence.outs: a slot's fence carries the slot's outcomes.
fence.floor: the fence carries each session's floor.
open.outs: the open takes the carried outcomes.
open.floor: the open takes the carried floors.
forward.once: a relay forwards a copy only once (A-21).
client-sessions.source: E-20 sess-smart ablation (experiments/E20-dedup/results/sess-smart-ablation.json: 13 counted) plus forward.once dropped alone on sess-fwd (results/sess-fwd-relay.txt: REFUSED in 9 steps); AMENDMENTS A-21
client-sessions.rows_note: MIN, RUST, SRV, LEAN, CELL, OBJ, MIN-P, MIN-TS, RLOG, EMB-V8, SIDE, COMP, the hybrids, BASE. All carry route-forward, so 14 is written in every row; 13 on the path of SRV's and EMB-V8's server clients (smart).
client-sessions.notes: The sess-fwd count is partly reasoned (E-20 could not run sess-smart's smallest model plus the relay under the state limit). High 16 adds: expire.silent (expire only after S silent ticks; the ablation dropped it because an early expiry is safe, but a build keeps it for usefulness, so it is not a correctness rule by DEV-10) and a reasoned rule that the registry's new writer gives every lease one election.ms to renew (E-22's E10 fix, if the same #sessions registry serves dedup). Overlap: apply.notin and refuse_r.notin are the base write path's write.dedup and refuse.dedup; the four carry rules are slot-move's final.outs. CALIBRATED: No count change. This record is now the one home of the dedup guard that E-17's base write path also wrote (write.dedup, refuse.dedup), and of the moves' carry of outcomes (E-17's final.outs, init.outs, merged.outs; rekey's final.outs).

rules: send.inflight: a producer has one attempt in flight per partition.
resend.horizon: the producer stops retrying R after the first send.
giveup.late: after R the attempt ends unknown.
forward.age: a relay takes the time it held a copy off the copy's budget.
restart.life: a restarted process takes a new producer id.
apply_next.known: apply the next sequence only when the writer holds state for (producer, partition).
apply_next.after: apply it only when its sequence is above the last.
apply_first.unknown: apply a first write only when there is no state for (producer, partition).
apply_first.budget: apply it only while the copy's budget is not spent.
refuse_next.known: refuse the next sequence only when the writer holds state for (producer, partition).
refuse_next.after: refuse it only when its sequence is above the last.
refuse_first.unknown: refuse a first write only when there is no state.
refuse_first.budget: refuse it only while its budget is not spent.
unknownpid.forgotten: answer unknown producer only once the forget has committed (A-22).
forget.silent: forget producer state only after it has been silent for P.
fence.state: a slot's fence carries the (producer, partition) state.
open.state: the open takes the carried producer state.
producer-state.source: E-20 pid-fwd ablation (experiments/E20-dedup/results/pid-fwd-ablation.json: 17 counted; pid-smart 16); Kafka KIP-98, KIP-360; AMENDMENTS A-22
producer-state.rows_note: ISR only. ISR carries fwd as well as smart, so 17; 16 on a smart-only path.
producer-state.notes: 1-minimal, not unique: another drop order keeps the epoch bump (KIP-360) and the 'unknown producer starts at 0' check instead, 18 rules (the high bound, E-20 section 2). Kafka itself needs those because it has no per-copy budget. Overlap: the apply/refuse guards include the base write path's dedup check, which ISR does not pay elsewhere (ISR carries no P mechanism from this batch). CALIBRATED: No count change. This record is now the one home of the dedup guard that E-17's base write path also wrote (write.dedup, refuse.dedup), and of the moves' carry of outcomes (E-17's final.outs, init.outs, merged.outs; rekey's final.outs). CALIBRATED: row_minus ISR 2: ISR's partitions never move (P fixN), so fence.state and open.state are not needed.

rules: A call with a key claims the key's row before its handler runs.
Only the claim's holder runs the handler.
The handler's result is stored in the key's row.
A retry with the same key gets the first stored result; the handler does not run again.
A new run starts only after the lease has lapsed, and it issues the same attempt ids as the first run, so writes the first run made are not applied twice.
The new run's writes carry a fence on the key (the claim's version), so the old runner's late writes are refused.
A key is kept for its TTL, and only then forgotten.
A call's copies belong to the caller's session (or issuer), so a copy that arrives after its key was forgotten is refused by that dedup option's own guard and never runs the handler again.
caller-keys.source: Catalogue rules text for caller-keys (judging/mechanisms.json: claim before the handler, store the result, a retry gets it, a re-run after the lease lapses issues the same attempt ids under a fence on the key); AMENDMENTS A-10; DESIGN-V5 4.5 'Call keys'; E-20 for the session binding (reasoned there) and for the 12 of the keys option alone
caller-keys.rows_note: Every row (A-10). In every row it sits beside another dedup answer (sess, win, pid, a transaction id, or JetStream's message ids), never alone.
caller-keys.notes: Count is the anchor's 12, but E-20 modelled keys as the whole dedup option for plain writes, not A-10's call keys beside sess or win, which was never modelled. Beside a dedup option, recv.latest, restart.life, refuse_f.first and the hop rules are already counted there. A reasoned count of the call-key layer's own rules is 8 (the low): the call claims its key's row before the handler runs; only the claim holder runs the handler; the result is stored in the key's row; a retry with the key gets the first stored result; the claim has a lease, judged by writer time; a re-run comes only after the lease lapses and issues the same attempt ids; the re-run's writes carry a fence on the key so the old runner's late writes are refused; the key is kept for its TTL. Under sess a call also needs a session of its own registered with its claim (E-20, reasoned), 9. High 14 is keys-fwd. CALIBRATED: 12 -> 9. E-20's 12 price keys as the whole dedup option for plain writes, which no row uses: every row has another option beside the key. Beside it, recv.latest, restart.life, refuse_f.first and the budget guards are that option's, and the key's carry is a row carried like any row. The 9 are the key layer's own rules (the catalogue's text) plus the binding to the caller's session. Low 8 drops the binding; high 12 is E-20's keys option alone. CHECKED: 9 -> 8 (skeptic F9). Dropped 'the claim has a lease, and it lapses by writer time': the lapse is writer-time's grant.lapsed, which lock-rows, queue-claims and consumer-groups also leave to writer-time. Low 7 drops the session binding. High 12 stays E-20's keys option alone.

rules: commit.acked: the consumer's cursor moves only after every output of the record is answered.
apply.above: apply an output only above the highest source sequence already applied here.
apply.mark: the output's entry records its source sequence (the mark).
fence.carry: an output slot's fence carries its marks.
open.carry: the open takes the carried marks.
srchi-marks.source: E-30 srchi-slot ablation (experiments/E30-derived-once/results/srchi-slot-ablation.json: 5 counted, 6 of 6 mutants); real Elle agrees on 2,800 histories; AMENDMENTS A-05
srchi-marks.notes: Keyed per (consumer, source slot, output slot): the per-group form loses an output on a slot move (E-30, 12 steps). The carry on a re-key, a split or a lane's range move was not modelled; high 6 allows one more rule where the moving unit is not a slot. CALIBRATED: row_minus 2 in LANE, ISR and BUY: fence.carry and open.carry serve only a moving partition, and those rows never move one.

rules: stamp.extrap: each peer's clock reading is carried forward by the receiver's own monotonic clock.
stamp.median: writer time is the median of the members' clocks, the writer's own included.
stamp.never_back: writer time never goes back: the max of that and the last time in the log, across a handover too.
expire.due: a row ends when writer time passes its TTL.
expire.log: an expiry is a record in the log, so every copy removes the row at one position.
grant.lapsed: a lease lapses when writer time passes its end.
writer-time.source: E-21 median1 ablation (experiments/E21-time/results/median1-ablation.json and results/handover.md: 7 needed on eight families); AMENDMENTS A-23

rules: A timestamp is physical time in ms plus a logical counter, and each one handed out is greater than the last.
Before handing out timestamps, the leader saves a window end (now plus about 3 s) to its store, and the save succeeds only while it still leads.
The leader never hands out a timestamp past the saved window end; it saves a new window first.
A new leader loads the last saved window end and starts above it.
The physical part never goes back: if the clock is behind, the leader keeps the last physical value.
When the logical counter runs out, the leader waits for the physical part to move on; it never wraps.
After making a timestamp the leader checks it still leads; a deposed leader returns an error, not the timestamp.
A row ends when oracle time passes its TTL.
An expiry is a record in the log, so every copy removes the row at one position.
A lease lapses when oracle time passes its end.

timestamp-oracle.notes: Rules 1 to 7 are the oracle, from PD's code. Low 6 is the oracle alone with the window rules (2 and 3) as one. High 12 adds: a client never hands a caller a timestamp it fetched before the call began (PD's client batches but never caches), and a leader that loses leadership resets its in-memory timestamp to zero. The Percolator rules for using timestamps (start and commit timestamps per transaction) belong to 2pc and txn, not here. Owner is fero when the row builds its own oracle, as these rows do; a row that ran PD itself would make it library. docs.pingcap.com could not be reached from this session.

rules: A member that cannot forward a write refuses it at once with a redirect; it never drops or holds it (A-02).
On a moved answer, the server takes the new owner from the answer or the routing record (#meta, or the resource's home log in the base) and forwards there, or passes the new address to the client.

rules: The client sends each write to the cached leader of its slot; on moved it takes the new owner from the answer, updates that entry and resends the same attempt.
On retry or no-writer (mid-move or mid-election) the client waits the retry-after and resends the same attempt; it never treats that answer as final.

rules: A client keeps at most its granted number of writes outstanding; the rest wait in the client.
A waiting write that reaches its deadline fails, and is then never sent.
The server hands each client or link its grant and shrinks it under load.

rules: Claim the unit's locks one at a time, in key order (claim.seq).
A claim writes the holder into the lock row (claim.lock).
The claim's new row version is the token, and the holder keeps it (claim.tok).
Once every lock is held, the holder moves on to the saga's intent (claim.pc).
A holder that learns its token is old releases every lock it still holds (giveup.release).
Then it starts again from the first claim (giveup.pc).

E-17's write.fence and E-21's pwrite.fence are fence-tokens' step.fence, counted there.

They give progress, not safety, so claim.free and giveup.lost are this record's high (8). The lease time comparison is writer-time's grant.lapsed (count-2), not counted here. A-10's 'a lock name has one lease' is the claim itself.

rules: A partition refuses a step whose token is below the highest token it has seen for that lock (step.fence).
A partition raises its highest token for a lock to the token of a write it takes; in saga rows the raise that matters is the undo's (undo.raise, E-24).

High 3 keeps step.raise apart from undo.raise.

rules: Write the intent only if the unit has none yet (begin.absent).
The begin writes the intent with direction run (begin.intent).
Begin only when no other unit is unfinished on my partitions (begin.noother).
Continue a found intent only at that point of the program (adopt.seq).
Continue only a unit that is found unfinished (adopt.unfin).
Continue it in its recorded direction (adopt.tgt).
Then go on from the step the intent shows (adopt.pc).
Resolve another unit only at that point of the program (other.seq).
Resolve another unit found unfinished on my partitions first (other.unfin).
Resolve it in its recorded direction, with my tokens (other.tgt).
Then go back to my own unit (other.pc).
If I lack that unit's locks, release mine and wait (backoff.release).
Run a step only in the run direction and in its turn (step.seq).
The step writes its change at its partition (step.data).
Then move to the next step (step.pc).
Handle a refusal only for the step just sent (fail.seq).
On a refusal, go to recording undo (fail.pc).
Record the direction only at that point (decide.seq).
Record undo in the intent row (decide.intent).
A write of the unit's direction to #sagas is refused when the token for the unit's first lock is below that lock row's version (decide.holds0).
The same write is refused when any other token it carries is below its lock row's version (decide.holdsN).
Start the undo at the unit's last step, so every step is undone, even ones that never ran (decide.pc, A-24).
Undo steps one at a time, backwards (undo.seq).
The undo writes the inverse change (undo.data).
Then move to the step before (undo.pc).
Record the end only after the last step or the last undo (close.seq).
Record done or undone in the intent row (close.intent).
A write of the unit's end to #sagas is refused when the token for the first lock is below that lock row's version (close.holds0).
The end write is refused when any other token it carries is below its lock row's version (close.holdsN).
Then the unit is over (close.pc).

rules: A transaction takes its start time from the oracle before it reads or prewrites anything.
The coordinator prewrites keys only while the transaction is in its prewrite phase.
After a prewrite answers ok, the coordinator moves on to the next key.
A refused prewrite ends the transaction, and the caller is told aborted.
The coordinator takes a commit time only after every prewrite has answered ok.
The commit time comes from the oracle after the last prewrite, so it is above the start time of any reader that saw the old value.
The primary key is committed before any other key.
The transaction is committed exactly when the primary's commit is in the log; the caller is told committed only then.
A refused primary commit (its lock is gone) tells the caller aborted.
Secondary keys are committed only after the primary's commit has answered ok.
A prewrite is refused while another transaction holds a lock on the key.
A prewrite is refused if the key has a commit newer than the transaction's start time.
A prewrite that finds this transaction's own lock answers ok again and locks nothing new.
A prewrite that finds this transaction's own commit or rollback record answers that outcome.
A prewrite writes a lock that names the primary key and the start time.
A prewrite writes the value under the start time, not yet visible.
A commit at a key happens only if the key still holds this transaction's lock.
The commit removes the lock.
The commit writes a commit record: the commit time pointing at the start time.
A retried commit that finds its own record answers it again: the transaction id is the dedup key.
A reader at time t never reads past a lock whose start time is at or below t: it waits, or resolves it.
A resolver checks the primary first, and only then changes the key it met.
At the primary, a lock still there is removed and a rollback record written, in one step.
If the primary has a commit record, the resolver takes its commit time from it.
If the primary has neither a lock nor a record, the resolver writes a rollback record there, so a late prewrite or commit is refused.
To roll a key forward, the resolver writes its commit record at the primary's commit time and removes its lock.
To roll a key back, the resolver removes its lock and its unseen value.
A resolver changes a key only while that key still holds that transaction's lock.
When a resolver rolls a transaction back at a secondary that holds neither its lock nor a record, it writes a rollback record there too, so a late prewrite at that key is refused.

two-phase-commit.rows_note: The PD family only (PD, PD+fix, TiKV-TS, TiKV-persisted), which build it in their own kernel (K kern).
two-phase-commit.notes: Never ablated: E-47 wrote these rules as its world and checked the memory rung, not 2PC's own rules. Counted at E-24's grain on purpose (program-order steps count, as 16 of the saga's 38 do), so 2PC and the saga compare fairly. Low 18 is Percolator's Figure 6 conditions and writes alone: no program-order rules (2, 3, 22) and no TiKV rollback record (14, 25, and the record half of 23), with commit's guard and updates merged. High 34 adds: a resolver rolls back only a lock whose TTL ran out, and the TTL and its keep-alive (progress, like E-24's claim.free); the coordinator rolls back its own prewrites on abort; a primary's rollback is kept as protected; and the two-update rules 23 and 26 split in two. The timestamps' source is timestamp-oracle (count-2); reading versions and collection are mvcc's; closed timestamps are their own. TiKV's async commit, one-phase commit and pessimistic locks are not in the row and not counted. CHECKED: 28 -> 29 (skeptic F14): rule 29 is the rollback record E-47's memrung.py res writes at a secondary with no lock and no record. High 35.

rules: A read at time t takes the newest commit record at or below t for the key.
It then reads the value stored under that record's start time.
A rollback record is never read as a version.
A delete is a version too: a read that lands on it sees no row.
The safe point is never above the start time of any live transaction or reader.
The safe point only moves forward.
Before collecting below the safe point, every lock older than it is resolved.
Collection keeps, for each key, the newest version at or below the safe point, and drops only older ones.
A delete at or below the safe point is dropped only when it is the newest version there, with everything older.
A read below the safe point is refused, since its versions may be gone.
mvcc.source: Percolator section 2.2 (data, lock and write columns) and TiKV's MVCC with its GC safe point, from memory; experiments/E47-memory-rung/models/memrung.py (reads at a snapshot time over write records; it leaves out clean-up of old versions)
mvcc.notes: The version itself is written by the commit record (two-phase-commit rule 19) and not counted again here. High 13 adds: rollback records and orphan values are collected only below the safe point and a primary's protected rollback is kept; a split or merge carries the safe point; and a snapshot read across ranges uses one start time. The LSM compaction that does the dropping is lsm-store's.

rules: A transactional id belongs to one coordinator, the leader of its transaction-log partition; any other broker refuses the request.
A producer that starts with a transactional id gets its producer id and a higher epoch.
Before that start is answered, the old producer's open transaction is aborted.
Every request carries the producer id and epoch, and the coordinator refuses an older epoch.
A partition is recorded in the transaction log before the producer's first write to it in the transaction.
A partition leader refuses a transactional write for a partition the coordinator has not recorded (KIP-890).
To end, the coordinator first commits prepare-commit or prepare-abort to its log; that record is the decision.
Once prepared, it writes a marker to every recorded partition, and a new coordinator after a failover finishes this from the log.
It records complete only after every marker is acknowledged.
A new transaction for the same id starts only after the last one is complete.
A transaction open longer than its timeout is aborted by the coordinator, with an epoch bump.
The epoch rises at every transaction end, so a late write of an ended transaction is refused (KIP-890).
ktxn-coordinator.source: Kafka KIP-98 (transaction coordinator, __transaction_state) and KIP-890 (server-side defence), from memory: not re-read, the pages were not reachable from this session; the local copy of Kafka's design page ('Using Transactions') read in this pass names markers and read_committed only
ktxn-coordinator.rows_note: ISR only, which builds Kafka's shape itself.
ktxn-coordinator.notes: Per-partition sequence dedup is producer-state's (count-2, 17), not here. Low 8 merges the epoch rules (2, 4, 12) and drops KIP-890's two (6, 12), as KIP-98 alone had them. High 15 adds sending offsets in the transaction (AddOffsetsToTxn and TxnOffsetCommit, 2 rules) and producer id expiry. The markers' partition side is ktxn-markers.

rules: A partition leader takes a marker only from the current coordinator: a marker with an older coordinator epoch is refused.
Each partition tracks the first offset of every open transaction.
The last stable offset is the lowest of those first offsets, and never above the high watermark.
A marker closes its producer's open transaction at that partition, so the last stable offset can move on.
A read_committed reader is served only up to the last stable offset.
An abort marker adds the transaction's offset range to the partition's index of aborted transactions.
A read_committed fetch returns the aborted ranges that its records overlap.
The reader skips the records of aborted transactions.
The reader never shows a marker to the app.
ktxn-markers.source: Kafka KIP-98 (control records, last stable offset, aborted transaction index), from memory; local copy of Kafka's design page (markers, read_committed) read in this pass
ktxn-markers.notes: The marker writes themselves are ktxn-coordinator's rule 8. Low 6 merges 6 with 7 and 8 with 9 and drops rule 1. High 11 adds: compaction and retention keep a marker until its transaction's records are gone, and a restarted partition rebuilds its open transactions from producer snapshots and the log.

rules: A write on a memory resource commits when a majority holds it in memory; the disks catch up in the background.
A transaction or saga with any key on a memory resource is refused before its first step (R2.txn).
A fenced write to a memory resource is refused (R2.put).
Lock rows live in #locks, which is never memory (R2.claim).
Session-bound rows, full history and derived outputs are refused on memory; the libraries keep their own state on persisted resources.
No system group (#meta, #locks, the other # resources) is ever memory.
A copy marks a clean stop only after it has fsynced its files on the same boot (judged by the boot id).
A copy without that mark does not vouch for its log and comes back as new, for that group's copy only, never the whole server.
When the oldest unsynced write on a server is older than 1 s, memory answers wait.
After a recovery of a memory group, a cursor of the old incarnation is refused unknown-log (the raise itself is meta-directory's rule 3).
A recovery raises the range generation or slot epoch, so a write copy sent before it is answered restored, final, and never judged again.
Split, merge and move entries on a memory group wait for disk, or the recovery adopts the table's view; no merge joins two resources.
fero recover --unclean restarts a memory group from the longest log any copy holds, never from a survivor alone.
The recovery takes the group's members and key range from the tables, not from what survived.
memory-rung.source: MEMORY.md 4.2 (form (a) with {R2}, rules 1-15) and 3.4; experiments/E47-memory-rung (R2.txn, R2.put and R2.claim model-checked as needed, results/sets.txt and greedy.txt; rule 15's longest log by brute force, results/raftcheck.txt)

In slot rows rule 2 refuses a saga, and rules 11 and 12 reuse restore-mark's session generation and the slot epoch, but the trigger is still this mechanism's.

Rule 8's 'comes back as new' is disk-incarnation's rule 2 with a new trigger; only the trigger and its per-copy scope are counted here. Low 8 is E-47's three refusals plus rules 1, 8, 11, 12 and 14. High 17 adds the oracle-time rule and splits rule 7 (judge by boot id; fsync then mark). E-24 and E-20 with a lost tail are still owed for the saga rows (MEMORY 4.4), so slot rows may need more. 'A failed background fsync or a full disk stops memory answers' is the journal's rules 12 and 15 (lsm-store's rule 17 in PD+fix and TiKV-TS): a condemned or full store stops every answer, memory ones too. Every memory row carries one of them. CALIBRATED: Rule 11 reworded: raising the incarnation is meta-directory's rule 3, which every memory row carries; the cursor check that routine recoveries make necessary stays here. No count change.

rules: Each subject is delivered through one ordering point: the shard that holds its slot.
A message goes to every subscriber registered there when it arrives, in order, at most once.
It is never written to the log, and its publish answers no more than sent.
When the subject's slot moves or its server goes, each subscription ends with a notice, so the client subscribes again elsewhere.
none-rung.source: REQUIREMENTS P-06; SPACE 2 Q none; AMENDMENTS 1.2 (K-10: its failover rule was never written or modelled); Redis 7 sharded pub/sub and core NATS, from memory
none-rung.rows_note: Every row. On BUY the outside system's core pub/sub does it (owner outside there).
none-rung.notes: Rule 4 is the failover rule nobody has written (K-10); it is counted because without it a subscriber silently stops receiving. Low 2 if routing and failover are taken from the subscribe path. High 6 adds: one live subscription per subject per client during a failover (so no duplicates), and a slow subscriber is cut with its reason rather than holding the stream.

rules: Journal writes run in order through one stream, so batches never land swapped.
An fsync covers only bytes written before it began; an entry waits for one that began after its write.
Each batch carries a chained sequence number; recovery stops at the first batch that lacks the next one, and never skips a bad batch to carry on.
Recovery finds a segment's end from the next segment's name, never from leftover bytes.
A torn or short record at the very end is cut: no fsync covered it, so nobody was told it committed.
A short write means ask again, not a torn record.
A follower writes a cut record (group, last offset kept) to the journal before entries that replace its tail.
Boot replays cuts in order and runs the chain check on the log as cut.
Segments and their indexes are written from synced journal entries, and an index entry points at exactly its record.
The journal is truncated only once the segments that cover it are fsynced.
Creating, renaming or unlinking a file fsyncs its directory.
One failed fsync condemns the store: it stops acknowledging, and its copies come back as new.
Data never writes into the reserve: only removes, votes, member changes, handovers and retention marks may use it.
A segment opened from the reserve is marked, so data cannot ride in behind the record that opened it.
Data writes are refused while free space is below the reserve plus room for one snapshot.
An unreadable journal record taints every group with a record after it, not only its own.
