journal.notes: Not counted here, counted elsewhere: writing entries to disk before acking (raft-log rule 8) and the leader counting its own copy only after its fsync (raft-commit rule 4); term and vote on disk before use (raft-term-vote rule 1); the per-entry checksum that turns damage into a wipe (disk-incarnation rule 1); one process per dir and epoch-named files (dir-lease); the recorder's journal rules (input-recorder). Rules 3 to 6 and 13 to 15 are A-09's format rules for every row, measured by E-29's power-loss tier; wal-per-group carries its own copies. SPACE priced only cuts and segment indexes (rules 7 to 10) as the journal's own. Low 10 drops the reserve trio (if priced row-wide), the dir fsync and rule 16. High 18 adds preallocated segments (a full disk then shows only when a segment is made) and 'if the reserve itself is full, stop voting and acknowledging'.

rules: Answer persisted only after the fsync that covers the row has returned.
Run the log's writes strictly in order through one queue, so rows never land swapped.
Each row carries a checksum and a link to the row before it.
At boot, a bad row with no valid row after it is a torn tail: cut there and stop.
A valid row after a bad one is damage: condemn the restore, empty the fold, and let the cluster teach the copy again.
A failed write, fsync or boot-record write latches the store: no later write, and persisted is never answered again.
A snapshot swap writes a temp file, fsyncs it, renames it, and only then moves the append handle to the new file.
Creating or renaming a file fsyncs its directory.
A short write means ask again, not a torn row.
Data never writes into the reserve: only removes, votes, member changes and retention marks may use it.
A segment opened from the reserve is marked, so data cannot ride in behind it.
Data writes are refused while free space is below the reserve plus room for one snapshot.
wal-per-group.source: shell/runtime.ts:382 (#ioq, ordered writes), 387 (#walFailed latch), 465-488 (persist: row, fsync, then persisted), 495-530 (snapshot swap), 537-560 (boot record), 581+ (restore: torn tail against interior damage); AMENDMENTS A-09 and experiments/E29-power-loss-disk-full for rules 9 to 12
wal-per-group.rows_note: ISR and V4. In V4 rule 6's fsync latch is also v4-latches' rule (count once: 11 there). ISR's Kafka-style partition logs add an offset index that must name exactly its record and recovery from the last recovery-point checkpoint (about +2, reasoned from memory).
wal-per-group.notes: Rules 1 to 8 are v4's code as it stands (low 8). Rules 9 to 12 are A-09's format rules, which apply to every row; the journal counts the same ones. Not counted: the boot record before the message it precedes (the vote rule of whichever consensus or ballot the row runs: v4-views in V4, raft-term-vote for ISR's controller); a non-empty log with no boot record is refused (a dir-identity rule, dir-lease's or genesis's). High 15 adds: segment end by the next segment's name if files are reused, preallocation, and the refusal of a log with no boot record. CALIBRATED: row_minus ISR 1: ISR also carries raft-log, whose rule 8 (write to disk before the ack) is this record's rule 1 for its metadata group; the journal leaves that rule to raft-log the same way. CALIBRATED: No count change. In V4 it is now the one home of the WAL chain check, the condemn on damage and the failed-fsync latch (v4-lanes and v4-latches no longer count them).

rules: A write goes to the write-ahead log before the memtable (acknowledging only once the log is synced is raft-log's rule 8, counted there).
A write batch is atomic: all of it in the log and the memtable, or none.
Each write gets the next sequence number, and the newest sequence wins for a key.
The last sequence number used is kept in the manifest, so a restart never reuses one.
A read looks in order: the active memtable, frozen memtables, level-0 files newest first, then each level, and stops at the newest version it may see.
Level-0 files are kept in sequence order; in every lower level, files never overlap in keys.
A flush writes a frozen memtable to a sorted file, fsyncs it, then records it in the manifest.
A log file is deleted only after every memtable holding its writes is flushed and recorded.
Every change to the set of live files is an edit appended to the manifest and fsynced; the CURRENT file points to the manifest and is swapped atomically.
Compaction keeps, for each key, every version a live snapshot or the safe point can still see.
Compaction drops a delete marker only at the bottom level, when no older version of the key can remain below it.
A compaction's outputs and the removal of its inputs land as one manifest edit.
An input file is deleted only when no live reader still uses it.
Recovery reads CURRENT, replays the manifest, then replays logs newer than the manifest's log number, stopping at a torn tail.
Every block and log record carries a checksum; a bad block is an error, never data.
Column families that must agree (lock, write and data) are written in one batch, and a log is kept until every family has flushed past it.
A failed background write (flush, compaction, full disk) puts the store into read-only, never on with a gap.
A reserve is kept on the disk and given up only when the disk fills (TiKV's reserve-space file).
While the reserve is in use, only writes that free space or keep the group alive (deletes, compaction output, votes, member changes and handovers) are taken.
Data writes are refused while free space is below the reserve plus room for one snapshot.
A short write means ask again, not a failed or torn write.
Creating, renaming or deleting a file fsyncs its directory.
One process per store: the LOCK file is held for the store's whole life, and a second open fails.
lsm-store.source: RocksDB's write path, flush, MANIFEST and CURRENT, compaction and recovery as TiKV uses them, from memory (no experiment ran an LSM); SPACE 2 S lsm; candidates/PD.md ('It copies TiKV with ... RocksDB')
lsm-store.rows_note: The PD family only. In PD the LSM also holds the Raft log (as TiKV's raftdb did); a row on raft-engine instead would move the log rules to a journal-like store.
lsm-store.notes: Only what correctness needs, not tuning (write stalls, bloom filters, compaction picking and rate limits are left out). Low 8 merges rules by stage: write (1-4), read (5-6), flush and log deletion (7-8), manifest (9), compaction (10-13), recovery and checksums (14-15). High 25 adds range deletes, merge operands, ingesting external files with a global sequence number (TiKV's region snapshots), snapshot pinning and release, the compaction filter that applies the safe point (counted in mvcc), and TiKV's disk-full reserve. Owned by the library (RocksDB or Pebble); a row that wrote its own LSM would pay all of these as fero. CALIBRATED: Rule 1 reworded so the ack-after-sync half is raft-log's rule 8 only, as the journal does. No count change. CHECKED: 17 -> 23 (skeptic F3). AMENDMENTS A-09 puts the reserve and 'a short write means ask again' on all rows, and the journal counts them at mid (its rules 6, 11, 13 to 15); this record left them in its high, so the borrowed store was counted coarser than fero's own. Rules 18 to 20 are the reserve, in TiKV's own code (owner fero in a PD row); 21 and 22 are RocksDB's (the short-write loop and the directory fsync); 23 is RocksDB's LOCK file, the PD rows' whole answer to dir-lease. Low 10 adds the reserve and the file-system rules as one stage each. High 30 is the old high's other seven items on the new 23.

rules: The leader uploads a segment or a snapshot with put-if-absent, under a name keyed by the group's incarnation and offset.
A segment or snapshot is named in the group's log only after its put is confirmed.
A snapshot layer holds the rows changed since the last one, plus a removal marker for each row removed since.
A cold start applies the base, then each layer in order, so a removed row stays removed.
A background merge folds layers in order, and drops a removal marker only once no older layer is below it.
A snapshot records which slots its group holds open at its offset, so a loaded copy never takes a moved slot's old rows as live.
A single incremental layer covers nothing by itself: only a merged base, or the copy's own full snapshot, lets the log be dropped.
A copy drops log below an offset only when that segment is uploaded or history allows dropping it.
It drops it only when no slot move still copies from it.
An object is deleted only when no log entry, merged base or reader still names it.
tier.source: DESIGN-V5.md 3.4 (snapshots are incremental layers) and 4.1 ('The object store', 'When a replica may drop its log below offset i'); judging/mechanisms.json rules text; E-28 (timing only)
tier.rows_note: Every +tier row (and the base). Rule 6 only in slot rows. Log-replica rows (V +wit: DRAFT, CELL, LANE, SPLIT) add the leader-stamped frontier: a log replica drops only below a merged base in the store or below what every full voter has snapshotted (+1).
tier.notes: Not counted, counted elsewhere: the snapshot is on disk or confirmed before any drop, and drops only below the snapshot's index (raft-snapshot rules 4 and 5, count-1); a copy acknowledges an installed snapshot only once fsynced (raft-snapshot rule 8); the parent may not drop what a fork names (forks). High 13 adds: only the leader uploads, the log-replica frontier, and the fork condition if forks is not carried. Low 6 merges the layer rules (3 to 5) into one and rule 10 into rule 2. CALIBRATED: row_minus 1 in LANE and ISR: rule 6 (a snapshot names the slots its group holds open) matters only where partitions move.

rules: A retry from a session older than the restore is refused (write.session).
A slot move records its new epoch in the store's mark before it uses it (move.hw).
A restore takes an epoch above the mark (restore.epoch).
A restore starts a new session generation (restore.sgen).
A cursor the history does not hold is refused (read.known).
restore-mark.source: experiments/E33-genesis-restore/README.md section 4 (restore design, 8 of 11 rules, 8 of 8 mutants); results/summary.md (restore)
restore-mark.bundle: E-33 restore 8 = restore-mark 5 + write.dedup (the dedup option's apply.notin) + write.seq and lock.seq (the row's position stamp: slot-sequence's write.pos, or lanes', rekey's or lineage's).
restore-mark.rows_note: Every row with a metadata group (A-08). In a row with no slots the epoch is the unit's generation or the resource's incarnation.
restore-mark.notes: Anchor as given. Three of the 8 are other mechanisms' rules seen from a restore: write.dedup is the dedup option's apply.notin, and write.seq and lock.seq are slot-sequence's stamp (count-2); so this mechanism's own rules are 5 (the low). Before calibration, high 9 added restore.hw (a restore records its own epoch in the mark), which dropped out only because the bounds had one restore. The model takes the store as always reachable. CALIBRATED: 8 -> 5. Three of E-33's 8 are other records' rules seen from a restore (count-3 flagged them); every restore-mark row carries a dedup option and a position stamp. High 6 adds restore.hw.

rules: Every full copy (writers, followers and replays) applies each committed record exactly once, in offset order, through data's hot lane; a client's apply is subscribe's gotrec rules.
Readers and subscribers see only the committed state; the log-end state with uncommitted batches is kept apart for judging and never shown.
The fold reads only the record and the rows: never the local clock, randomness or local settings; time comes from the record's writer time.
A user function that throws while a record folds (a view, a tap, a subscriber) is reported as a fault and never stops the fold or changes what it applies (V4-47).
fold-all.source: DESIGN-V5.md 4.3 ('Two states on the writer', 'The fold'); Raft paper section 5.3 (apply in log order), from memory; DECISIONS V4-47 and api/substrate.ts's Fault seam for rule 4
fold-all.rows_note: Every F all row. fold-leader repeats these five where F is ldr.
fold-all.notes: Not counted, counted elsewhere: followers, readers and replays never re-run a check, op or rule, and a new leader folds its whole log before it judges (writer-judging rules 4 and 5, count-2); a copy resets its fold from a snapshot (raft-snapshot rule 10); answering only once the fold reached a read's index (raft-readindex rule 4, subscribe). Rule 5 overlaps slot-move's final.recs and subscribe's bopen.fold: it is the fold side of the same carry. Low 3 drops rules 4 and 5; high 6 (7 before calibration) adds the two writer-judging rules if that mechanism is not carried. CALIBRATED: 5 -> 4. Rule 5 (a moved slot's rows live in one group) is the move's carry of rows (final.recs, init.rows, merged.rows, rekey's final.rows), counted there. row_minus V4 1: in V4, 'each change once, in order' is v4-lanes' rules 3 and 4.

rules: Every full copy (writers, followers and replays) applies each committed record exactly once, in offset order, through data's hot lane; a client's apply is subscribe's gotrec rules.
Readers and subscribers see only the committed state; the log-end state with uncommitted batches is kept apart for judging and never shown.
The fold reads only the record and the rows: never the local clock, randomness or local settings; time comes from the record's writer time.
A user function that throws while a record folds (a view, a tap, a subscriber) is reported as a fault and never stops the fold or changes what it applies (V4-47).
A follower that keeps the log only never answers a state read; it sends the reader to the leader or the standby.
A failover hands leadership to the standby first.
A new leader that is not the standby rebuilds its fold from a snapshot and the tail before it answers or judges.
When the standby is lost, the leader names a new one and warms it from a snapshot and the tail.
fold-leader.source: SPACE 2 F ldr and 3 R1.LF; AMENDMENTS A-26 (the standby is required: a cold rebuild passes F-05's 2.5 s above about 560,000 rows, E-05); DESIGN-V5.md 4.3 for the five base rules
fold-leader.rows_note: LEAN, SIDE (the app folds) and OBJ. No row carries both fold-all and fold-leader, so the five base rules are counted here, not twice.
fold-leader.notes: Rules 1 to 5 are fold-all's base, repeated because these rows do not carry fold-all. Rules 7 and 9 guard F-05's failover bound (A-26), not safety; low 5 (6 before calibration) drops them and rule 4. High 10 (11 before calibration) adds a leader transfer that waits until the standby's fold has caught up, and 'never pick a log-only follower as a transfer target'. CALIBRATED: 9 -> 8, the same move as fold-all's rule 5.

rules: A lazy follower answers a read at position p only after it has folded up to p; it folds on demand to get there.
A lazy fold that has fallen behind what the log still holds restarts from the latest snapshot, never across a gap.
fold-lazy.source: SPACE 2 F lazy (1 novel); judging/mechanisms.json rules text; precedents Neon's pageserver and TiKV's follower read, from memory
fold-lazy.rows_note: OBJ only, beside fold-leader, which holds the base fold rules.
fold-lazy.notes: No experiment. Rule 1 overlaps the general read rule (subscribe's 'never before its fold reached the cursor'; fero's reads from any replica); the lazy part is folding on demand. Low 1 counts only that; high 3 adds 'a lazy follower folds only up to the commit offset it has learned' if the base rule is not taken as covering it.

rules: Each group's log holds a committed entry naming the fold version in force from that offset.
The version names data's exact build (a digest that moves with the fold), not SCHEDULE_VERSION.
It also names fero's way in: the L2 library and the seam's repairs.
A copy never folds an entry under another version than the one in force at its offset.
A copy that cannot run the version in force refuses to serve until it can.
A roll raises the version only after every copy has said it can run it.
A copy whose data or Node version would fold a record differently is refused before any copy stops, naming the pair (DEP-10).
fold-version.source: REQUIREMENTS OPS-12 and DEP-10; experiments/E43-fold-versions/README.md 'What the fold version must pin' (measured: two builds that both say SCHEDULE_VERSION 4 fold differently); AMENDMENTS A-10 (five pins)
fold-version.rows_note: Every row. For V4 only if v4 were built on.
fold-version.notes: E-43's pin 3 (user functions run at the writer only, their results in the log) is writer-judging's 'append only results'; pin 5 (bounds on one record) is writer-judging's size check; neither is counted here. Pin 4 (F-21 hashes rows, never views) belongs to the divergence check. Low 4 merges rules 2 and 3 and drops rule 7. High 9 adds: clients that fold check the version too, and a Node change restarts every copy together where user functions run in the fold.

rules: A server sends a snapshot only from a loaded fold (snap.loaded).
It sends a snapshot only once its fold has reached the subscriber's cursor (snap.cursor).
It sends the snapshot itself (snap.send).
A server sends a record only from a loaded fold (rec.loaded).
It sends a record only up to its fold, so committed records only (rec.committed).
It sends the record itself (rec.send).
A server that cannot serve yet answers retry: go elsewhere with your cursor (notready.send).
A replica that lacks the reader's next record says so (expire.lost).
It answers END, and only the leader of the group that holds the slot answers expired (expire.send, A-06).
The subscriber handles a snapshot only when one has come for it (gotsnap.is).
A snapshot first clears the subscriber's whole view (gotsnap.clear).
Then it puts in the snapshot's rows (gotsnap.rows).
Then it sets the cursor to the snapshot's position (gotsnap.cursor).
The subscriber takes a record only if it is the next one after its cursor (gotrec.is).
It applies the record once (gotrec.apply).
It moves its cursor on by one (gotrec.cursor).
It frees the credit the record used (gotrec.credit).
On retry it leaves that server (gotretry.leave).
On retry it gives back its credit there (gotretry.credit).
It subscribes again elsewhere, with its cursor (connect.link).
It treats expired only when that answer came (gotexp.is).
Expired ends the reader (gotexp.dead).
The new group also gets the names of the old group's segments below the fence, so it can serve log readers behind it (bopen.segs).
A client's write resolves only once it has committed (resolve.committed).
And only once the client's own subscription has passed the write's position (resolve.seen).
Then the write is resolved (resolve.res).
subscribe.source: experiments/E31-subscribe/README.md sections 2 and 3 (26 by ablation, 27 with bopen.segs by segs_check.py); results/summary.md
subscribe.bundle: E-31: 26 by ablation, 27 with bopen.segs = subscribe 26 + bopen.fold, which is the move's carry of rows (slot-move final.recs), counted there. This record is also the one home of E-17's five base read rules (read.committed = rec.committed; read.after and read.next = gotrec.is; read.take = gotrec.apply; read.cursor = gotrec.cursor).
subscribe.rows_note: 27 in rows whose slots move (the slot and pslot rows, the base). 26 where no slot move carries segment names (PD, ISR, LANE, CELL, SPLIT; their own carry across a re-key, a split or a lane move was not modelled).
subscribe.notes: Overlaps to count once: rec.committed, gotrec.is, gotrec.apply and gotrec.cursor are slot-table's read.committed, read.next, read.take and read.cursor (count-2, fixN's base reads); bopen.fold is slot-move's final.recs. Before calibration, low 22 was 27 less those five. The conflated diff path is a speed path and not counted. High 29 (30 before calibration) adds the cursor rules E-31 did not exercise (it had no unclean recovery): a cursor whose cluster id or incarnation does not match, or whose slot epoch is older, is refused unknown-log; a newer epoch is answered retry. CALIBRATED: 27 -> 26. bopen.fold is slot-move's final.recs (count-3 flagged it). bopen.segs stays here; rows whose slots never move get row_minus 1 for it. Before calibration, low 21: less the four rules that are also E-17's reads, if those were counted in the partition records instead.

rules: A leader's lease starts when it sent the round that a majority acked, not when the acks came back.
The lease ends before the followers' election timeout runs out, less the clock drift bound.
The leader answers a lease read only while the lease is unexpired by its own monotonic clock.
A leader that starts a leader transfer, sees a higher term, or steps down stops lease reads at once.
read-lease.source: Ongaro's thesis section 6.4.1 (leases), TiKV's leader lease and etcd's ReadOnlyLeaseBased, from memory; SPACE 2 W lease (no experiment, G-25)
read-lease.rows_note: PD family (W lease ridx) and OBJ (W lease any, where the lease is the writer lease held by compare-and-swap on the store, obj-writer-lease).
read-lease.notes: Overlaps: rule 3 is the prevote and check-quorum guard (raft-prevote-checkquorum; raft-term-vote's high); the own-term half of rule 4 is raft-readindex rule 1 and rule 5 is raft-readindex rule 4. In the PD rows, which carry raft-readindex, the lease's own rules are 1, 2 and 6 (the low 3). High 9 adds TiKV's suspect lease after a merge, a split's new range taking no lease until its leader has one, and a new leader waiting out the old lease after a transfer. CALIBRATED: 6 -> 4. 'No vote while the leader is heard' is raft-prevote-checkquorum's rule 3; 'only after an entry of its own term' and 'from a fold at the commit offset' are raft-readindex's rules 1 and 4. In OBJ the same two come from obj-writer-lease and fold-lazy. count-3's low 3 had dropped the lease's own clock check too; it stays.

rules: A checksum on every entry finds damage below the tail, and the copy acts on it: in a rejoin row it wipes itself and comes back new; in a par row it marks the entry bad, and par-repair's rules fetch it.
disk-incarnation.source: experiments/E37-bad-entry/README.md section 2 (Z rejoin: 2 rules, each shown needed by cut1-obs or silent1, and ghost1-obs)
disk-incarnation.bundle: E-37: rejoin's 2 = disk-incarnation 1 + raft-config rule 15 (a wiped or new disk never votes as the copy it replaced; E-37 says E-14's GhostReturn is this rule). par's 7 = par-repair 6 + this record's checksum rule (E-37's ParDetect).
disk-incarnation.rows_note: Every rejoin row and every par row (the COMP2 and MIN-P+par hybrids, TiKV-TS, TiKV-persisted, the base). Every row that carries it also carries raft-config, which holds the ghost rule. In par rows the check's action is par-repair's mark, not a wipe.
disk-incarnation.notes: E-37 is not a split of one total: rejoin (2) and par (7) are separate counts. The torn-tail rule ('only a tail the checksum shows was never acknowledged is cut') is counted in the storage mechanism (journal rule 5, wal-per-group rule 4); high 3 counts it here. Adding the new copy back as a learner is healing's. CALIBRATED: 2 -> 1. The ghost rule is raft-config's rule 15 (the same rule, E-37), counted there. The checksum rule now names both actions, so par rows count the check once. High 3 = the ghost rule here plus the torn-tail cut that the journal counts.

rules: A copy with a bad entry grants no vote.
A copy with a bad entry does not stand for election.
It repairs only from a peer whose commit index is at least the bad entry's index, so the peer knows it committed.
It repairs only from a peer whose own copy of that entry is not bad.
The repair copies the entry.
The repair clears the bad mark.
par-repair.source: experiments/E37-bad-entry/README.md section 3 (7 rules, each shown needed by a mutant; 8 of 9 mutants caught); results/mutants.md
par-repair.bundle: E-37 par 7 = par-repair 6 + ParDetect, which is disk-incarnation's checksum rule (every par row carries disk-incarnation; in a par row that rule marks the entry bad).
par-repair.rows_note: The par rows: the COMP2 and MIN-P+par hybrids, TiKV-TS, TiKV-persisted, and the base (V5-6).
par-repair.notes: Taking appends while damaged was shown not needed. ZIgnore (a damaged copy drops vote and append requests unanswered) stayed undecided; E-17's convention would keep it (high 8). Before calibration, high 9 also added PAR's 'possibly committed' query for damage above the copy's own commit point, which E-37 did not model. Rule 1 is the same checksum as disk-incarnation's rule 1 in rows that carry both. CALIBRATED: 7 -> 6. ParDetect (the checksum marks the entry bad) is disk-incarnation's one rule, which every par row carries; counted there.

rules: The controller hands the writer role over only when the current writer is gone to it (handover.gone).
It hands the role only to a server that is up and linked (handover.alive).
It hands it over by committing a writer entry with the next epoch in the group's log (handover.append).
A server takes the role only through a committed writer entry that names it (takeover.named).
On taking the role, the server takes that entry's epoch as its own (takeover.wep).
The log group's leader takes an append only if it carries the latest committed writer epoch (write.epoch).
writer-epoch-rlog.source: E-16 results/rlog-ablation.json and models/rlog.py; E-16 README 'RLOG's 9 rules'; AMENDMENTS A-14
writer-epoch-rlog.bundle: E-16 rlog 9 = writer-epoch-rlog 6 + takeover.fold (writer-judging rule 5: fold to the log end before judging) + write.append (slot-table's write.append) + write.fold (fold-all rule 1). RLOG carries all three.
writer-epoch-rlog.rows_note: RLOG only. It sits on top of controller-commands (C cent-co), which E-16 counts apart.
writer-epoch-rlog.notes: Anchor as given: 9 of 9 non-equivalent mutants caught. The ablation dropped two written rules (handover.other, and write.holder, which the epoch check covers); the pinned bounds are not rules. Low 7: write.append and write.fold are the write's own append and fold, which in other rows sit in raft-log and fold-all; RLOG carries both of those keys too, so a calibrator may take them out here. The controller's command list, its epoch check and its timeout are controller-commands'. CALIBRATED: 9 -> 6 (count-4 named two of these as its low). Low 5 merges takeover.named and takeover.wep; high 7 adds write.holder.

rules: The writer numbers entries in order and sends each one to every log node of the loglet's current node set.
A log node writes an entry to disk before it acks it.
The committed point moves to the highest entry that, with every entry before it, has reached an ack quorum.
Each append carries the writer's committed point, and the log node keeps it, so recovery and readers can learn it (F2).
A writer that is told 'sealed' stops writing to that loglet for good.
When a log node fails, the writer takes it out of the ack counts of every entry above the committed point.
It then resends those entries, in order, to the replacement nodes.
loglet.source: BookKeeperProtocol.tla (github.com/Vanlightly/bookkeeper-tlaplus, main, read here): ClientSendsAddEntryRequests, ReceiveAddConfirmedResponse with MaxContiguousConfirmedEntry, ClientReceivesAddFencedResponse, ChangeEnsemble, ResendPendingAddOp; V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F2; Delos (OSDI 2020) from memory
loglet.bundle: SLOG's shared log (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): loglet 9, loglet-seal 12, loglet-chain 8, writer-epoch-slog 7, total 36 from BookKeeper's TLA+ spec (Vanlightly, BookKeeperProtocol.tla) and V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F1-F7
loglet.notes: Rule 2 is not in the TLA+ spec (it has no crashes); BookKeeper's journal does it. The log node's 'refuse a normal append once sealed' is loglet-seal's rule 1. The metadata swap of a node-set change is loglet-chain's rule 2. Low 7 merges rules 7 and 8 and drops rule 9 where readers only go through the writer. High 10 splits 'resend in id order' into its own guard, as the spec writes it. CALIBRATED: 9 -> 7. 'Answer only after commit' is slot-table's write.append and 'readers read only committed entries' is subscribe's rec.committed; SLOG carries both.

rules: A sealed log node refuses every normal append to that loglet.
A log node seals a loglet when asked, even one it has never seen.
A recoverer seals the loglet's last node set, and starts reading only once the sealed nodes cover every possible ack quorum.
It starts reading just after the highest committed point the sealed nodes report.
It reads from the node set the loglet had when recovery began, never from one changed since.
Its reads seal too, so an entry that was half written cannot reach an ack quorum behind it.
One node that holds an entry is enough to recover it.
An entry counts as absent only when enough nodes say 'no entry' to cover every ack quorum; a silent node is never a 'no' (F1).
If neither answer is reached once every node has answered or timed out, recovery stops and starts again later.
Each recovered entry is written again, in order, to a write quorum, and the end is fixed only after every one is acked.
A sealed node still takes a write that is marked as a recovery write.
A reader of a sealed loglet that is not closed yet reads only up to the last stamped committed point (F2).
loglet-seal.source: BookKeeperProtocol.tla (github.com/Vanlightly/bookkeeper-tlaplus, main, read here): BookieSendsAddConfirmedResponse/AddFencedResponse, BookieSendsFencingReadLacResponse, ClientReceivesFencingReadLacResponse, ClientSendsRecoveryReadRequests (HasQuorumCoverage), ReadStatus/ReadPositive/ReadNegative/ReadUnknown, ClientWritesBackEntry, RecoveryClientClosesLedger; V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F1, F2, F4
loglet-seal.bundle: SLOG's shared log (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): loglet 9, loglet-seal 12, loglet-chain 8, writer-epoch-slog 7, total 36 from BookKeeper's TLA+ spec (Vanlightly, BookKeeperProtocol.tla) and V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F1-F7
loglet-seal.notes: Every rule but 12 is a guard or update in Vanlightly's spec, whose comments say why each is needed (rules 2, 5 and 6 are named there as needed for correctness; rule 8 is the 'unknown is not absent' rule that F1 cites). Rule 12 is F2's reader rule, not in the spec. The swaps that mark recovery and close the loglet are loglet-chain's. Low 9 merges 8 with 9, 7 with 10, and drops 12 where readers go through the writer. High 13 adds 'the recoverer stops taking late seal answers once it starts reading'.

rules: The chain changes only by compare-and-swap on its version.
A writer's node-set change is written, starting at its committed point plus one, by that swap before the writer goes on.
A recoverer first marks the loglet 'in recovery' by a swap.
Node-set changes made during recovery reach the chain only in the close.
A close fixes the loglet's end by a swap; whoever loses that swap stops and adopts the winner's end (F4).
The next loglet starts at the closed end plus one, in the same swap that closes the old one (F5).
A reader finds a position's loglet through the chain, and never reads a closed loglet past its end.
loglet-chain.source: BookKeeperProtocol.tla (github.com/Vanlightly/bookkeeper-tlaplus, main, read here): ChangeEnsemble (meta_version check), ClientClosesLedgerSuccess/Fail, ClientStartsRecovery, RecoveryClientClosesLedger; V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F3, F4, F5, F7; Delos VirtualLog and Pulsar's managed ledger from memory

loglet-chain.rows_note: SLOG only. The chain lives in the metadata group, whose Raft rules are the raft-* keys.
loglet-chain.notes: Rules 1 to 5 are the metadata half of BookKeeper's protocol (the spec's meta_version and meta_status). Rule 6 (F5) and rule 8 (F7) come from the review, not the spec. Low 6 merges 3 into 5 and drops 7 as routing. High 9 splits rule 5 into the close's guard and the loser's adopt. CALIBRATED: 8 -> 7. 'Delete a loglet's copies only once a merged snapshot past its end is named and uploaded' is tier's rules 7 and 8, which SLOG carries.

rules: The controller names a new writer only once the old writer's session has lapsed.
It names only a server that is live and linked.
It commits the new writer, with the next epoch, in the metadata group.
A server takes the writer role only through that committed entry.
The new writer recovers and closes the old writer's open loglet before it opens its own.
Only the writer changes its own log nodes; the controller changes only writers (F3).
writer-epoch-slog.source: SPACE 4.1 footnote 5; V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F3, F4; matched to E-16's RLOG rules (results/rlog-ablation.json) as the template; Pulsar's topic ownership from memory
writer-epoch-slog.bundle: SLOG's shared log (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): loglet 9, loglet-seal 12, loglet-chain 8, writer-epoch-slog 7, total 36 from BookKeeper's TLA+ spec (Vanlightly, BookKeeperProtocol.tla) and V5-LOG-FIRST-REVIEW F1-F7
writer-epoch-slog.notes: Rules 1 to 4 and 6 have the same shape as E-16's handover.gone, handover.alive, handover.append, takeover.named and takeover.fold. The seal (rule 5, whose steps are loglet-seal's) takes the place of RLOG's per-append epoch check. The controller's command machinery is controller-commands'; the session lapse is controller-sessions'. Low 5 drops rule 2 (liveness) and rule 7 (F3 says the two-reconfigurer race is safe by the swap, only wasteful). High 8 adds 'the new writer takes the epoch of the entry', as RLOG's takeover.wep. CALIBRATED: 7 -> 6. 'Fold to the recovered end before judging' is writer-judging's rule 5, which SLOG carries.

rules: A member registers with the controller and gets a new, higher epoch each time.
It keeps its session alive by heartbeats.
The controller fences a member whose heartbeats stop for the session timeout, by a committed entry.
A fenced member gets no role (leader, writer, in-sync member, log node) until it registers again.
A request that names a member's epoch is refused unless it is that member's current epoch.
A new controller leader gives every session a full timeout from its own start before it fences anyone.
controller-sessions.source: SPACE 2 C (failure detector: sessions to the controller); Kafka KIP-631 broker registration, heartbeats and broker epochs, and TiKV store heartbeats to PD, from memory; E-25
controller-sessions.rows_note: PD, ISR, SLOG and the C=cent hybrids (COMP+par C=cent V=full, MIN-P+par C=cent V=full, PD+fix, TiKV-TS, TiKV-persisted). For PD-family rows that run TiKV's own PD this would be owner library; the study's PD row builds it, so fero.
controller-sessions.notes: Rule 4 also carries Kafka's 'only an unfenced replica may join the in-sync set' (KIP-841), so isr-set does not count it again. Rule 6 is liveness and F-06 (no false failovers); KRaft resets every broker's last contact when a controller becomes active (from memory), as E-22's E10 fix does for leases. Low 4 drops rules 5 and 6. High 7 adds the controlled-shutdown path (a member asks to leave; the controller moves its roles before it fences it).

rules: Only the replica that believes it leads takes producer writes and appends them.
A follower fetches from the leader and appends records in offset order, right after its own log end.
The leader takes each follower's log end from the offset in its fetch.
isr-log.source: Kafka's replication TLA+ (github.com/hachikuji/kafka-specification, master, read here): KafkaReplication.tla, Kip279.tla, Kip320.tla: LeaderWrite (KafkaReplication.tla:202), FollowerReplicate (:302), FencedFollowerFetch (Kip320.tla:49)
isr-log.bundle: Kafka ISR replication (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): isr-log 3, isr-set 8, high-watermark 7, leader-epoch 10, eligible-leaders 6, total 34 from Kafka's replication TLA+ (KafkaReplication, Kip279, Kip320) and Kafka 3.9.0's PartitionChangeBuilder.java; controller-sessions 6 sits beside it (also carried by PD and SLOG); the controller's command list is controller-commands'
isr-log.notes: The epoch on each record and the fetch's epoch check are leader-epoch's. The disk side (append and fsync) is wal-per-group's. Rule 3 is implicit in the spec's high-watermark guard (it reads followers' logs directly); a builder must write it. Low 2 folds rule 3 into high-watermark. High 4 adds 'a follower fetches only from the replica its current leader-and-ISR names'.

rules: The leader drops a follower from the in-sync set when it does not follow the leader's epoch or lags behind the leader's log end.
The leader adds a follower only if it follows the leader's current epoch.
It adds it only once it has caught up to the high watermark.
It adds it only once the leader's high watermark has reached the start of the leader's own epoch (KIP-320).
An add names the follower's current broker epoch, and the controller refuses a stale one, so a broker that restarted and lost data cannot rejoin (KIP-903).
An in-sync set change is committed only if the current leader sends it at the current partition epoch (a compare-and-swap).
The controller removes a fenced broker from every in-sync set.
While a change is in flight, the leader counts the larger of the old and new sets for the high watermark.
isr-set.source: Kafka's replication TLA+ (github.com/hachikuji/kafka-specification, master, read here): KafkaReplication.tla, Kip279.tla, Kip320.tla: FencedLeaderShrinkIsr (Kip320.tla:78), FencedLeaderExpandIsr with HasFollowerReachedHighWatermark and HasHighWatermarkReachedCurrentEpoch (:87-117), QuorumUpdateLeaderAndIsr (KafkaReplication.tla:213), ControllerShrinkIsr (:158); KIP-841, KIP-903 and KIP-497's maximal ISR from memory
isr-set.bundle: Kafka ISR replication (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): isr-log 3, isr-set 8, high-watermark 7, leader-epoch 10, eligible-leaders 6, total 34 from Kafka's replication TLA+ (KafkaReplication, Kip279, Kip320) and Kafka 3.9.0's PartitionChangeBuilder.java; controller-sessions 6 sits beside it (also carried by PD and SLOG); the controller's command list is controller-commands'
isr-set.notes: Rules 1 to 4, 6 and 7 are guards in the TLA+ spec (Kip320's header lists rule 4 as one of the four rules it found). Rules 5 and 8 are from memory of KIP-903 and KIP-497. 'Only a registered, unfenced replica may join' is controller-sessions' rule 4. Before KIP-966 the controller kept the last member in the set; with eligible leaders the set may empty (eligible-leaders). Low 6 drops rule 1 as liveness (shrinking only lets the high watermark move) and rule 8. High 9 adds the pre-KIP-966 'never empty the set' guard for rows without eligible leaders.

rules: The leader moves the high watermark only to an offset every in-sync member holds.
It moves it only once every in-sync member has fetched in the leader's current epoch.
A follower sets its own high watermark to the lower of the leader's high watermark and its own log end.
A follower that cuts its log lowers its high watermark to at most the cut.
A write with acks=all is answered only when the high watermark passes it.
A write with acks=all is refused while the in-sync set is smaller than min.insync.replicas.
high-watermark.source: Kafka's replication TLA+ (github.com/hachikuji/kafka-specification, master, read here): KafkaReplication.tla, Kip279.tla, Kip320.tla: FencedLeaderIncHighWatermark (Kip320.tla:63), FencedFollowerFetch (:49), FencedBecomeFollowerAndTruncate (:134), KafkaReplication.tla's StrongIsr; acks=all and min.insync.replicas from Kafka's documented producer contract, from memory
high-watermark.bundle: Kafka ISR replication (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): isr-log 3, isr-set 8, high-watermark 7, leader-epoch 10, eligible-leaders 6, total 34 from Kafka's replication TLA+ (KafkaReplication, Kip279, Kip320) and Kafka 3.9.0's PartitionChangeBuilder.java; controller-sessions 6 sits beside it (also carried by PD and SLOG); the controller's command list is controller-commands'
high-watermark.notes: Rule 2 is KIP-320's 'the leader bumps the high watermark only if followers in the ISR have acknowledged the leader and its epoch'. KIP-966's 'the high watermark moves only while the set is at least min.insync' is eligible-leaders'. Low 5 drops rules 3 and 4 where followers never serve reads (W ldr). High 8 adds 'a new leader serves reads only after its high watermark reaches its own epoch's start' (Kafka answers OFFSET_NOT_AVAILABLE then; from memory). CALIBRATED: 7 -> 6. 'Readers see only records below the high watermark' is subscribe's rec.committed (serve committed records only), which ISR carries.

rules: The controller elects a new leader only from the in-sync set.
Each leader change raises the leader epoch, committed in the controller's log before any replica acts on it.
A replica acts on a leader change only if its epoch is above the one it holds.
Each record carries the epoch of the leader that wrote it.
Each replica keeps the start offset of every epoch it has seen.
A follower that takes a new epoch asks the leader where the last epoch they share ends, before it fetches.
It asks only a leader that is at its own epoch.
The leader answers with where that epoch ends in its own log.
The follower cuts its log to that offset.
Every fetch carries the follower's epoch, and the leader refuses a fetch from another epoch.
leader-epoch.source: Kafka's replication TLA+ (github.com/hachikuji/kafka-specification, master, read here): KafkaReplication.tla, Kip279.tla, Kip320.tla: ControllerElectLeader (KafkaReplication.tla:176), ControllerUpdateIsr (:138), BecomeLeader (:186), LogRecords with epoch (:82), FencedBecomeFollowerAndTruncate and FirstNonMatchingOffsetFromTail (Kip320.tla:134, Kip279.tla), FencedFollowerFetch (Kip320.tla:49); KIP-101, KIP-279, KIP-320
leader-epoch.bundle: Kafka ISR replication (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): isr-log 3, isr-set 8, high-watermark 7, leader-epoch 10, eligible-leaders 6, total 34 from Kafka's replication TLA+ (KafkaReplication, Kip279, Kip320) and Kafka 3.9.0's PartitionChangeBuilder.java; controller-sessions 6 sits beside it (also carried by PD and SLOG); the controller's command list is controller-commands'
leader-epoch.notes: Kip320's header names rules 6-7 (truncate before fetching, from a leader at the same epoch) and rule 10 as what the model found. Electing from the eligible list when the set is empty is eligible-leaders'. Electing only an unfenced broker is controller-sessions'. Low 8 merges 4 with 5 and 6 with 8. High 11 adds KIP-320's consumer side: a reader that sees its position's epoch end earlier detects the cut and resets.

rules: While the in-sync set has at least min.insync members, the eligible list is empty.
When a change leaves the in-sync set below min.insync, the replicas it drops join the eligible list.
A replica that rejoins the in-sync set, or is elected from the list, leaves the list.
A broker says at registration whether it shut down cleanly; one that did not leaves the list.
The controller elects from the eligible list only when the in-sync set is empty.
The leader moves the high watermark only while the in-sync set has at least min.insync members.
eligible-leaders.source: Kafka 3.9.0 metadata/src/main/java/org/apache/kafka/controller/PartitionChangeBuilder.java (read here): maybePopulateTargetElr (line 554), isValidNewLeader (line 331), tryElection's ELR branch (lines 343-347); KIP-966 from memory for rule 6
eligible-leaders.bundle: Kafka ISR replication (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): isr-log 3, isr-set 8, high-watermark 7, leader-epoch 10, eligible-leaders 6, total 34 from Kafka's replication TLA+ (KafkaReplication, Kip279, Kip320) and Kafka 3.9.0's PartitionChangeBuilder.java; controller-sessions 6 sits beside it (also carried by PD and SLOG); the controller's command list is controller-commands'
eligible-leaders.notes: Rules 1 to 5 are read from Kafka's controller code. Rule 6 is KIP-966's high-watermark condition, from memory (the KIP page was not reachable here). Low 5 folds rule 4 into controller-sessions' registration. High 8 adds the last-known-leader list for unclean recovery and 'an unclean election clears the list'.

rules: The writer creates log object N+1 only if it does not exist yet (If-None-Match).
A write is committed when, and only when, that PUT succeeds (the answer after commit is the write path's write.append).
A writer whose PUT finds the object already there has lost its role: it stops and re-reads the manifest, and never writes that number again.
A PUT whose answer was lost counts as unknown: the writer reads the object back before it answers or moves on.
Readers read log objects in number order and stop at the first missing number.
obj-log.source: SPACE 2 R obj, Q put; E-28 (If-None-Match measured on MinIO); Delta Lake's log protocol (VLDB 2020, section 3) and SlateDB's WAL objects, from memory
obj-log.bundle: OBJ's object-store log (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): obj-log 5, obj-manifest 6, obj-writer-lease 6, total 17, reasoned from Delta Lake's log protocol, SlateDB's manifest and S3 conditional writes (from memory) and E-28
obj-log.notes: Deleting log objects below the manifest's start is obj-manifest's. The new writer's first claim of the next number is obj-writer-lease's. Low 4 merges 2 into 1. High 7 adds 'each log object names its writer epoch, and the fold skips an object from an older epoch' and a size cap per object.

rules: The manifest changes only by a conditional PUT on the version that was read (If-Match).
Every change of writer, snapshot or log start goes through that one object.
After a failed swap, the server re-reads the manifest and decides again; it never retries the same swap blindly.
A swap whose answer was lost is read back before anything acts on it.
A snapshot is named in the manifest only after its own PUT succeeded.
Log objects below the manifest's log start are deleted only after the snapshot that covers them is named there.
obj-manifest.source: SPACE 2 R obj (manifest CAS), SPACE 4.1 footnote 7; E-28 (If-Match measured on MinIO); SlateDB RFC 0001 (manifest) and Iceberg's pointer swap, from memory
obj-manifest.bundle: OBJ's object-store log (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): obj-log 5, obj-manifest 6, obj-writer-lease 6, total 17, reasoned from Delta Lake's log protocol, SlateDB's manifest and S3 conditional writes (from memory) and E-28
obj-manifest.rows_note: OBJ only. In OBJ the manifest swap is also the controller's register (C cent by CAS); controller-commands counts the healing commands apart.
obj-manifest.notes: Rules 4 and 5 are the same kind of rule as obj-log's rule 4 and DESIGN-V5 4.1's 'a snapshot is named only after its put is confirmed'. Low 4 merges 3 with 4 and folds 2 into 1. High 7 adds 'placement changes go through the manifest too'.

rules: A server becomes the writer only once the old lease has run out, by its own clock plus the skew margin.
It takes the role by swapping the manifest with a higher epoch and a new lease end.
Before it judges any write, it claims the next log number, so the old writer's next PUT fails.
The writer renews the lease by a swap before the lease ends.
It stops writing, and stops serving lease reads, once it cannot renew in time: the lease end minus a margin.
obj-writer-lease.source: SPACE 2 R obj (lease epochs), SPACE 3 B0.O.L; E-25; SlateDB's writer_epoch and fencing write, Kubernetes Lease objects, Gray and Cheriton 1989, from memory
obj-writer-lease.bundle: OBJ's object-store log (no model count; split here so no rule is counted twice): obj-log 5, obj-manifest 6, obj-writer-lease 6, total 17, reasoned from Delta Lake's log protocol, SlateDB's manifest and S3 conditional writes (from memory) and E-28
obj-writer-lease.notes: Rule 3 is SlateDB's fencing write as remembered (a new writer writes the next WAL object so the old one's PUT fails); without it the old writer can still commit one object after the takeover. Rule 6's lease reads are read-lease's mechanism; only the writer's stop is counted here. Rule 1's clock check (own clock plus the skew margin) is counted here; writer-time's rules stay apart. Low 4 merges 3 into 2 and 5 into 6. High 7 adds 'a lease is never renewed by a writer that has seen a higher epoch'. CALIBRATED: 6 -> 5. 'Fold to the end before writing' is writer-judging's rule 5, which OBJ carries.

rules: fero's glue: A resource is a stream that keeps only the last message per subject, one subject per row, so a write publishes the whole row, never a change.
fero's glue: A row's version is the stream sequence of its last message.
fero's glue: A conditional write or op publishes with the expected last subject sequence it read; on a refusal it reads again and tries again.
fero's glue: A retried op first checks whether the row's last message carries its attempt id; if so the first try landed, and it answers that.
fero's glue: The message id names one try, never the whole attempt, because a refused publish burns its id on a clustered stream.
fero's glue: A lost answer is retried with the same message id, so inside the dedup window it cannot land twice.
fero's glue: Every client folds the whole stream in order, from the start, through an ordered consumer.
fero's glue: A write answers only once the stream acked it and the client's own fold has passed its sequence.
fero's glue: A delete is a marker message, and a create-if-absent after a delete expects the marker's sequence, not 0.
fero's glue: A lock lives in a stream whose maximum age is its lease, so one lock name has one lease length.
fero's glue: A queue is a work-queue stream with a pull consumer whose ack wait is the lease and whose delivery limit is the queue's.
fero's glue: A take hands over what it has at once; it never holds messages while it fills a batch.
fero's glue: The dead-letter move copies a message to the dead stream and then deletes it, and a scan of what is left at or below the last handed-out sequence catches a missed advisory.
fero's glue: FIFO per partition uses one consumer per partition.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-log 1): Only the leader adds new entries to the log.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-log 2): Each new entry carries the leader's current term.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-log 3): An append names the index and term of the entry just before its first entry.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-log 4): A follower refuses an append or a snapshot from an older term.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-log 5): A follower takes the entries only if it holds an entry at that index with that term.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-log 6): Where a new entry's term differs from the one held at its index, the follower cuts its log from there.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-log 7): A follower never cuts entries that match; it adds only the ones it lacks, so a late or repeated append cannot shorten its log.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-log 8): A replica writes entries to disk before it acks them.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-log 9): A follower acks the exact index up to which its log now matches the leader's.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-log 10): After a refused append, the leader steps back and resends from earlier until the logs meet.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 1): Term and vote are on disk before any message that depends on them goes out.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 2): A follower or candidate stands when its election timer runs out with no word from a leader; hearing a leader or granting a vote restarts the timer.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 3): Election timeouts have a random part, so two replicas rarely stand at once.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 4): On standing, a replica raises its term by one.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 5): It votes for itself in that term.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 6): It clears its vote tally from earlier terms.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 7): A replica grants a vote only to a request for its own current term.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 8): It grants at most one vote per term: only if it has not voted, or voted for the same candidate.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 9): It grants only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date: a higher last term, or the same last term and at least as long.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 10): A granted vote is recorded as the replica's vote for that term.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 11): A candidate counts a vote reply only if it is for its current term.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 12): A candidate adds each granted vote to its tally.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 13): Only a candidate can become leader; a follower with an old tally never does.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 14): Any message with a higher term makes the receiver take that term.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 15): On a higher term, a leader or candidate steps down to follower.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 16): On a new term, the replica clears its vote.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-term-vote 17): A candidate that hears from a leader of its own term becomes its follower.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-commit 1): On winning, the leader resets what it knows each follower holds: its own log end for itself, nothing for the others.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-commit 2): The leader counts an append ack only if it is from its current term.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-commit 3): A success ack raises what the leader knows that follower holds.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-commit 4): The leader counts its own copy only once its own fsync has landed.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-commit 5): The commit index moves to the highest index that a majority of the configuration holds.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-commit 6): The leader commits by counting only an entry of its own term; earlier entries commit with it.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-commit 7): A heartbeat carries a commit index no higher than what that follower is known to hold.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-commit 8): A follower raises its commit index only up to the last entry it knows matches the leader's log.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-snapshot 1): A replica cuts a snapshot only at an index it has applied.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-snapshot 2): A snapshot records the index and term of its last entry.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-snapshot 3): A snapshot holds the configuration in force at that index.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-snapshot 4): A replica writes the snapshot to disk before it drops any log below it.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-snapshot 5): A replica drops log entries only below its snapshot's index.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-snapshot 6): The leader sends its snapshot to a replica that needs an entry it has dropped.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-snapshot 7): A follower ignores a snapshot at or below its commit index.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-snapshot 8): A follower uses a received snapshot only once all of it has arrived and is on disk.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-snapshot 9): If the follower's log holds the snapshot's last entry, same index and term, it keeps the entries after it; otherwise it drops its whole log.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-snapshot 10): The follower resets its fold, its configuration and its commit index from the snapshot.
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 1): A candidate counts only the votes of its own configuration's voters (r01).
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 2): A new leader sets its pending-change mark at its log end, so it waits for older changes (r02).
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 3): A new leader first adds an empty entry of its own term (r03, Ongaro's 2015 fix).
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 4): Only a leader proposes a membership change (r04).
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 5): A leader proposes a change only once its last change is committed (r05).
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 7): A change goes into the log as an entry (r08).
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 8): Proposing a change sets the pending-change mark (r09).
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 9): A replica applies the latest committed configuration (r17).
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 10): A leader that the applied configuration removes steps down (r18).
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 11): No member stands while a committed change is still unapplied (r20, the campaign guard).
JetStream's Raft (as raft-config 13): A configuration takes effect when it commits, not when it is appended.
JetStream's Raft: a step-down names a caught-up peer as the next leader, if it can.
JetStream's Raft: the named peer stands at once on the transfer entry, without waiting for its timer.
JetStream's Raft: while it steps down, the old leader takes no new proposals.
JetStream's Raft: a transfer that does not finish leaves the group to a normal election.
JetStream's Raft: an observer never stands for election.
JetStream's Raft: the leader sends the log to observers as to other peers.
JetStream's Raft: the leader tracks when it last heard from each peer.
JetStream's Raft: a leader that has not heard from a quorum for the lost-quorum interval steps down.
Meta group: stream and consumer assignments are entries in the meta group's log, and a server builds or drops its copies only from committed assignments.
Meta group: a stream's replicas go on distinct servers that match its cluster and tags and have room.
Meta group: a consumer's replicas go on its stream's peers.
Meta group: a create with an existing name and a different config is refused.
Meta group: a server taken out of a stream's peers deletes its copy only once the new assignment has committed.
Meta group: when a server is removed for good, the meta leader moves each of its stream and consumer copies to another server.
Stream: the stream's leader gives each stored message the stream's next sequence.
Stream: a publish whose message id is in the duplicate window gets the first ack and is not stored again.
Stream: message ids are forgotten once they are older than the duplicate window.
Stream: the duplicate window's ids are rebuilt from stored messages after a restart or a leader change.
Stream: a publish with an expected last sequence is refused unless the stream's last sequence matches.
Stream: a publish with an expected last subject sequence is refused unless that subject's last message has that sequence.
Stream: the leader judges these expectations against everything it has proposed, not only what is applied, so two racing publishes cannot both pass.
Stream: with one message kept per subject, storing a message removes that subject's older message.
Stream: a message older than the stream's max age is removed.
Stream: under work-queue retention a message is removed once its consumer acks it, and two consumers may not overlap on a subject.
Stream: a publish is acknowledged only after its entry has committed in the stream's group.
Stream: a deleted or purged message is removed through the stream's log, on every copy.
Consumer: delivered and ack-floor changes go through the consumer's own group, so a new consumer leader resumes from them.
Consumer: each delivery raises the message's delivery count.
Consumer: a message not acked within the ack wait is delivered again.
Consumer: a message whose delivery count reached max deliver is not delivered again.
Consumer: the ack floor moves only over a run of acked sequences with no gap.
Consumer: an ack for a message that is not pending changes nothing.
Consumer: a pull request is answered only with messages not pending with another puller.
Consumer: an ordered consumer that sees a sequence gap or misses heartbeats starts a new consumer from the last sequence it saw.
Store: messages are written to block files, each record with a checksum.
Store: with sync always, a block write is fsynced before the entry is acked.
Store: at start each block is scanned, and a bad record at the end is a torn tail and is cut.
Store: a per-subject index is rebuilt from the blocks when its file is missing or stale.
Store: a removed message is marked deleted, and its space comes back only by compaction.
Store: the stream state saved in a snapshot is checked against the blocks at start.

rules: The main thread sends every message for a group to that group's one worker.
A group runs on one worker only, never on two at once, and stays there while it lives in the process.
A group's entries all go to its worker's journal, and boot replays each worker's journal into the same groups.
Messages between workers are recorded as kernel inputs, so a replay sees them in the same order.

rules: The daemon appends only what the app returned for a batch; it never judges or folds a client write itself.
Each result carries the term it was judged in, and the daemon drops a result whose term has ended.
A ring slot is reused only after the reader has released it.
side-seam.source: SPACE 2 H side; AMENDMENTS A-30 (a ring, not a socket); E-03 (measured); Aeron Cluster's IPC between the consensus module and the service, from memory
side-seam.notes: No durable state. Two more rules apply across the seam but are counted elsewhere: the app folds to the log end before it judges after a restart or a new term (writer-judging's rule 5), and a client is answered only after the daemon reports commit (the base write path). High 5 counts them here as well, since SIDE must rebuild them across a process line. Low 1 keeps rule 1 only (A-30's seam).

rules: A call runs only on the host whose app folds its partition, the partition leader's host; any other host forwards it there.
A call cut off by a leader handover is refused with retry, or re-run at the new leader under its call key; it never finishes on the old leader's fold.
leader-calls.source: SPACE 2 U ldr; AMENDMENTS section 2 U; E-22 (U ldr buys no safety: conditions are judged at the writer anyway)
leader-calls.notes: No durable state. E-22 found that running a call at the leader adds no safety; in SIDE it is needed because only the leader's host folds the partition (F ldr). Writes caught in a transfer are route-forward's rule 2; a re-run's dedup is caller-keys'. Low 1 keeps rule 1. High 3 adds 'a call reads its rows only from a fold at or past the commit of its own earlier writes'. CALIBRATED: Writes caught in a transfer are raft-leader-transfer's rule 2 (route-forward's old rule 2).

rules: A process that pools tenants counts each tenant's big-record bytes per second against its budget.
Past the budget it holds the tenant's bytes back, in order, and never drops them.
tenant-budget.source: AMENDMENTS A-29; E-35 (measured the ratios; the budget was not built); REQUIREMENTS SC-11 and OPS-14; Kafka's quotas (KIP-13), from memory
tenant-budget.rows_note: DRAFT, CELL, LANE, SPLIT, SLOG, OBJ, RLOG (N tier) and EMB-V8 (N pool). Not the base (N proc). A volume per tenant needs no rule.
tenant-budget.notes: The property is SC-11's p99 bound (a neighbour at its quota raises another's p99 by at most 10%), a performance bar, not safety: so low 0, as admission-credits and move-policy take it. Rule 2's 'never drops, in order' is what keeps the hold-back from breaking F-01 or per-partition order. High 3 adds OPS-14's fsync budget per project.

rules: The create of the cluster id in the object store succeeds only while no id is stored there (If-None-Match) (found.absent).
The seed whose create succeeds writes that id and founds #meta as its only voter (found.create).
Every other seed adopts only the id it finds stored (adopt.stored).
A seed that adopts keeps that id in its dir and joins as a replica through healing (adopt.adopt).

Under V5-2 and V5-3 (the base) there is no #meta: the winner founds the project's first resource or the directory's seed instead, and the same create-if-absent rule holds (reasoned). Per-resource conditional creates are meta-catalog's rule 1, not this one.

rules: fero init runs once; a second init is refused (init.once).
Init mints the cluster id (init.mint).
A seed never founds by itself; it adopts only an id it finds at a seed it reaches (join.adopt).

rules: The lock record is put in place in one atomic step: written whole to a side file, then hard-linked onto the lock's name.
The lock is taken before the boot record is read.
A lock from another machine is never taken over.
In the same pid namespace, the holder is live while its pid lives with the start time the record names; otherwise the lock is stale.
In another pid namespace, the holder is judged by its lease alone: stale only once the lock went untouched for a whole lease.
Before it calls a lock stale, the look waits for the next touch, up to the rest of the lease.
The holder touches its lock from a thread of its own, never from a timer on the main loop, so a long replay cannot starve the lease.
The toucher touches a lock only while the record is still its own; a foreign record means it was taken over, and it says so and stops.
A takeover runs under a marker file, claimed the same atomic way, so two heirs cannot both take the dir.
Under the marker the heir looks at the lock again, and gives way if a live holder came meanwhile.
A stale marker is removed by a rename and a look at what came, never by a plain unlink.
A release removes only a record that is still this process's own.
Taking the dir takes a new, higher epoch.
A holder writes only files whose names carry its own epoch.
A new holder renames the old epoch's directory to retired-<epoch> before it reads it.
It writes and fsyncs a boot record naming that directory and the end offset before it reads.
It reads the retired directory read-only, and never past that end.
Files roll by a new file and an unlink, never by truncating in place.

dir-lease.rows_note: Every row that keeps fero's own dirs (16 study rows, the hybrids, the base). Rules 1-12 exist in v4 today and would be ported; rules 13-18 are new in v5.
dir-lease.notes: Rules 1-12 are the V4-59 mutations that guard 'one holder at a time' or 'a gone holder can be taken over'; V4-59's other mutations (an unguarded stderr write, a missing error or exit listener, the name in a refusal) keep the node alive or the message right, not the property, and are left out. Directory fsyncs are the journal's. Low 12: rules 13-18 plus the six core lock rules (1, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12), for a world with no containers. High 22 adds: a refusal after the lock gives it back; a new lease thread is fed every lock still held; a thread that cannot start gives the lock back; an mtime in the future counts as one lease from now. CHECKED: Basis by rule (skeptic F7): rules 1 to 12 are code (V4-59); rules 13 to 18 are reasoned from DESIGN-V5 4.1 (6).

rules: A member keeps its row in #groups alive by renewing its lease; a member whose lease lapses by writer time is dropped.
Every change of the live members raises the generation, in the same entry.
Each member works out its shares with one pure function of the live members and the generation, so all agree and each share has one owner per generation.
A new owner reads the share's committed cursor fresh, and starts from there.
Before it reads the source, the new owner writes the cursor once under its own generation, so an older owner's late commit is refused.
Every cursor commit carries a fence on the member's generation.
consumer-groups.source: E-22 patterns/lib/group.ts (read here: tryTake, rebalance, batchOf.commit); DESIGN-V5 5.3 'Consumer groups'; REQUIREMENTS P-08; Kafka's group coordinator (KIP-848), from memory
consumer-groups.rows_note: Every row but V4 and BUY (BUY uses JetStream's own consumers, inside outside-log).
consumer-groups.notes: E-30 modelled the cursor and the marks, not the membership. Counted elsewhere: the cursor moves only after every output is answered, and the marks and their carry (srchi-marks); the refusal of an older token at the cursor row's writer (fence-tokens); the lapse comparison (writer-time). E-22 builds ownership from one #locks row per share whose version is the token; DESIGN-V5 uses a generation in #groups; the rules map one to one. Rule 5 is what makes P-08's 'a paused member cannot commit' hold before the new owner's first commit. Low 4 drops rule 3 as balance (a second owner is fenced and its outputs dedupe) and merges 4 into 5. High 8 adds: a member stops work on a share it lost; it hands a share back only between batches with nothing uncommitted.

rules: A client renews its session's lease in #sessions while it lives.
A session's lapse is written as an entry in #sessions' log, so every writer sees it at one position.
A new #sessions writer gives every lease at least one election.ms to be renewed before it lapses any (E-22's E10 fix).
A row written while: 'session' carries its session's id.
A writer takes such a row only once the session's record has committed, and refuses one bound to a session it does not know (E-22's F2 fix).
Each group's writer follows #sessions, and removes a lapsed session's rows by entries in its own log, only after the lapse has committed there.
A write bound to a session whose lapse the writer has already seen is refused, so no row outlives its session.
presence-rows.source: DESIGN-V5 5.3 'Presence'; E-22 API-NOTES D10 and fixes E10 and G2/F2 (proto/l2.ts, measured on P-13); REQUIREMENTS P-13; AMENDMENTS K-11; ZooKeeper ephemeral nodes and etcd leases, from memory
presence-rows.rows_note: Every row but V4 and BUY.
presence-rows.notes: The lapse comparison (writer time past the lease end) is writer-time's grant.lapsed. In rows with D sess the same #sessions registry also serves dedup: client-sessions counts only its dedup rules (apply.live, expired.dead), so rules 1-3 are counted here once; client-sessions' high names rule 3 as the one it would share. writer-judging's high names rule 5 as belonging here. Rule 3 carries P-13's 'a live session's rows are never removed' (E-22, seed 27). Low 5 merges 2 into 6 and drops 7 if the follow is exact. High 8 adds: a method's write bound to the caller's session needs the caller's process to keep that lease (E-22 API-NOTES). CALIBRATED: row_minus 1 in the sess rows and the base: one #sessions registry serves both, and rule 7 (refuse a write of a lapsed session) is client-sessions' apply.live there.

rules: Every frame carries its sender's protocol version.
The cluster version is raised only once every member runs a kernel that can speak it.
A member whose kernel cannot speak the cluster version is refused, at join and at HELLO.
Members write entries and frames only in the cluster version's format, not their own newest, until the version is raised.
Once raised past a format change, the cluster version is never lowered; a roll can be undone only before then (OPS-12).
cluster-version.source: DESIGN-V5 4.2 'Mixed versions' and the #meta record table; REQUIREMENTS OPS-12; Kafka's metadata.version (KIP-778) and CockroachDB's cluster version, from memory
cluster-version.rows_note: Every row with a metadata group, the hybrids and the base. Under V5-2 (the base) there is no #meta: the version lives in each resource's own log, or the processes compare it in HELLO only (reasoned); the rules stay.
cluster-version.notes: Not modelled. The fold's version per group is fold-version's, apart from this. Low 3 keeps rules 1-3 (rule 4 is how 2 is used). High 6 adds: the raise checks the member list as committed, so a member that joins during the raise is checked too.

rules: Each side's HELLO carries a fresh random nonce.
A proof is an HMAC over both nonces, the prover's side of the link, and the verifier's id and address, so it cannot be replayed or sent back.
A peer is let in only after its proof checks, compared in constant time.
A node with a secret refuses a peer without one, and a node without one refuses a peer that has one.
Member verbs are taken only on links that passed the door; admin asks also need the admin key.
While a rotation runs, a proof under either the current or the next secret is taken.
The old secret is dropped only after every member holds the next one.
The CA key is kept only as envelopes encrypted to each #meta voter's key, and a voter change re-wraps them.
A join token is single-use: a committed #meta entry spends it before the member gets its certificate.
Each member gets its own certificate, signed by the CA, at join.
A removed member's certificate is revoked in #meta, and every handshake checks the revoked list.
A client checks a server's certificate against the CA fingerprint in its own credential.
cluster-credentials.source: v4 kernel/door.ts (read here: proofMsg, prove, verify, ctEq, doorMatrix; DECISIONS V4-30, DESIGN-DOOR) for rules 1-4; DESIGN-V5 4.1 'Member verbs only on member links' and 4.5 'Identity and security' for rules 5-12; Docker swarm mode's PKI, from memory
cluster-credentials.rows_note: Every row with a metadata group, the hybrids and the base. Under V5-2 and V5-3 (the base) there is no #meta, and V5-3's directory keeps no log, so the CA envelopes, join tokens and revocations need another home (each resource's own log, or a small project log); this is open.
cluster-credentials.notes: Rules 1-4 are v4's door (code) and stay. TLS itself is node:tls (a library) and is not counted. The client token signed by the cluster (ctx.peer) is left out; high 14 adds it and its expiry check. Low 8 merges 1 into 2, 6 into 7, 10 into 9, and drops 12 as the client's own check.

rules: A claim takes only rows with no live lease: never claimed, or the lease has lapsed by writer time.
It takes them in order, the first n of the partition (FIFO per partition).
A claimed row's lease ends at writer time plus the lease length.
The claim raises the row's delivery count in the same entry.
An ack, nack or extend goes through only with the claim's token (its version), so a worker whose lease lapsed cannot touch the next taker's claim.
Past the delivery limit, a row is first written to the dead-letter resource (only if absent there), then removed from the queue.
A take hands over what it has claimed at once; it never holds claims while it waits to fill n (A-10).
A claim that finds nothing appends nothing to the log.
queue-claims.source: E-22 patterns/lib/queue.ts (read here: takeOnce, toDead, msg.ack/nack/extend); DESIGN-V5 5.3 'Queue'; REQUIREMENTS P-09; AMENDMENTS A-10; E-44 (the take-at-once rule found on JetStream); Amazon SQS and Redis Streams' XCLAIM, from memory
queue-claims.rows_note: Every row but V4 and BUY (on BUY the claim is JetStream's ack wait and delivery count, inside outside-log).
queue-claims.notes: Counted elsewhere: an empty claim's answer waits for the commit of the log end it was judged on (writer-judging rule 2); the lapse comparison (writer-time); the claim op as a single step at the writer (writer-judging). Rule 7 carries P-09's 'held by at most one live lease' (E-44 handed jobs out twice inside a lease without it). Rule 8 is P-09's 'an empty take writes nothing'. Low 5 drops rules 2, 7 and 8. High 10 adds a due time ('at', by writer time) and cron's ack-and-next in one write (P-22).

rules: A fork writes one record per group, naming the parent's snapshot and segments and the position it starts from; it copies nothing.
A fork starts only at a position the parent has committed.
It refuses a position below what the parent has already dropped.
Its record commits before it reads any of the parent's files.
The parent drops a snapshot or segment only after checking that no committed fork record names it.
Each slot comes from the one group that held it open at the fork's cut, so a slot that was moving then is neither lost nor doubled.
A fork writes only new files under its own name and incarnation; it never overwrites or deletes the parent's.
forks.source: DESIGN-V5 6.2 piece 8 and 4.1 ('no fork references it'); REQUIREMENTS TEST-06, OPS-07; E-06 (measured cost only); Neon's branches (ancestor timeline and LSN, GC keeps what a branch needs, a branch below the GC cutoff is refused), from memory
forks.rows_note: Every row with a metadata group, the hybrids and the base. Under V5-2 the fork's records live in the new resource's own log and the pins in the parent's log (reasoned).
forks.notes: Not modelled and not built (API.md: TEST-06 open). Rules 3-5 together close the race between a fork and the parent's retention, as Neon's GC cutoff check does. Erase's 'erased' marker in forks is OPS-13's and not counted. Low 4 merges 3 into 2 and 4 into 5. High 9 adds: a fork's pins go when the fork is deleted (space, not safety); a cursor from the parent is refused on the fork.

rules: Every kernel input is recorded, in order, before the kernel steps on it.
An input is recorded as a whole frame, never as a socket chunk.
Bulk bytes are recorded by a reference into the journal, which holds them in arrival order.
The journal keeps every segment the recorder's window refers to, or a dump copies them out first, before compaction drops them.
input-recorder.source: E-42 README (measured: 18 of 18 replays byte for byte; the chunk-boundary finding) and pipeline.ts's recorder; AMENDMENTS A-09 (three recorder rules); REQUIREMENTS OPS-11 (d)
input-recorder.rows_note: Every row with a deterministic kernel of fero's own (18 study rows, the hybrids, the base); not V4 or BUY.
input-recorder.notes: A-09 counts rules 2-4 as format rules; rule 1 is the recorder's own write rule. That every source of nondeterminism (ticks, completions, ids) reaches the kernel only as an input is the deterministic kernel's own discipline (DEV-07), not counted here. Replaying under the fold version in force is fold-version's. Messages between workers are worker-map's. Low 3 is A-09's three. High 5 adds 'object-store completions are recorded too' (OPS-11 lists them; E-42 did not build them).

rules: Each life of a member writes under its own lane: the bare id in its first life, id~n after a restart, so a new life never reuses an old life's tickets.
The owner adds each change it stamps to the end of its own lane, so a lane only grows in ticket order.
On a plain (unscoped) node, a received change at or below its lane's applied mark is a duplicate and is dropped.
A change above the mark is added to its lane whether or not it wins its cell, and the applied and shippable marks move up to it.
On a scoped node or a client, a change at or below the applied mark may fill a gap: drop it if the lane already holds that ticket, else insert it at its ticket's place so the lane stays in order.
A lane holds each (author, ticket) once: a teacher's fold skips tickets already there and raises the applied mark to the lane's tail, so the fast path never adds a ticket twice (V4-56).
On replay, a WAL row at or below the applied mark is skipped; a fresh one moves the applied, shippable and durable marks together.
