rules: A stamp is (view number, ticket, author); compare the view number first, then the ticket, then the author.
The owner stamps each change with the next tick of its Lamport clock and its committed view number.
The clock moves up to every ticket the node sees, even on changes it then drops.
On restart, the clock is rebuilt from every replayed stamp.
Before it stamps past the ceiling saved on disk, the owner saves a new ceiling first (the clock lease), so a restart never reuses a ticket.
A change takes its cell only if its stamp is strictly newer than the cell's stamp; a loser is skipped but still counts as received.
A field cell loses to any ancestor (its row or a parent field) stamped at or above it (V4-18).
A winning write sweeps every field cell under it that is stamped at or below it: the field leaves the state and takes the writer's stamp.
Field cells under it that are stamped above it stay, and are put back on top downstream.
After a field remove, levels that only the removed field had made up are taken back, so every node shows the same row.
A committed write that loses its cell is reported lost to the writer waiting on it, since no apply will ever carry it.
v4-stamps.source: kernel/node.ts:3087-3088 (newer), 1179 and 1183-1186 (stamp site, clock lease), 2813-2897 (apply: 2818 the election, 2839 ancestors, 2878-2895 the sweep, 2896 #reapply, 2897 #unvivify), 2822 and 2841 (lost); kernel/write.ts:803 (merge-up), 995 (replay rebuild)

v4-stamps.rows_note: Rules 7 to 10 come from overlapping cells (V4-18), which every v4 node runs.
v4-stamps.notes: Low 6 is the plain LWW register with a Lamport clock (rules 1-6). Rules 7-10 are V4-18's field-level cells: real guards, each fixed after a found bug, but a v5 that folds whole rows would not need them. Rule 10 is a projection repair (#unvivify); its many sub-cases (arrays, scalars) count as one rule here. Rule 11 carries the write-outcome promise (V4-7), not cell safety; a calibrator may move it to the write path. High 12 splits the sweep's tombstone half out. A remove's tombstone itself is counted in v4-tombstones.

rules: A digest tells, for each lane, the ticket of the last entry held: exactly what this node can serve.
Every admitted link starts with a digest exchange: the lower id asks, the other answers, so both sides heal.
An answer ships, lane by lane in ticket order, every entry above the peer's tail, then replies with its own digest when asked.
A link is marked synced only when the answer's ship is complete; live changes go only on synced links, so they never jump ahead of the missing suffix.
After a paused link drains, a link that dropped frames or skipped a digest opens a new exchange, never into a full queue.
An answer that stopped at a full queue keeps a cover at the peer's tails, leaves the link unsynced, and resumes first at the next drain; its reply goes only after the whole ship.
On a plain cluster, the lower id also asks on every heartbeat, to heal any loss that gave no signal.
On a scoped cluster, an answer to a member ships nothing: history reaches a member only by a teacher and the floor handshake.
A client digests only its primary feeder; digests on its other links are not answered.
A server drops records that arrive on a client link: a spoke never teaches.

A spoke whose applied mark on any lane is above its feeder's tail (or that fails over to a scoped feeder while holding anything) wipes its fold, remembers the cells it showed, and asks for everything with a new ask id.
A resync ends only on a reply whose ask id is at or above the resync's own.
At a resync's end, each remembered cell that did not come back, and is not under a live or remembered ancestor, is taken off the screen.
A drain digest toward a client says it dropped frames, so a spoke whose ask got no reply asks again.
A clear on a synced client link leaves a ceiling below every record it took; it caps the spoke's next digest, and the spoke keeps it across a failover until a reply.

rules: On a plain node, a lane's frontier is the lowest crash-stable mark over every member of the committed view; nothing above it is cut.
A crash-stable mark is: for this node, its durable mark if it has a disk, else its applied mark; for a peer that ever sent durable marks, its durable mark, else its shippable mark.
With no committed view (open genesis) there is no frontier, and nothing is cut.
At or below the frontier, keep exactly the entries that still win their cell, with their first stamp and attempt id; drop the rest.
On a scoped node, a slice's entries are cut only if the slice is held and sealed here with no latch open.

They are cut only at or below F: the lowest crash-stable attested floor over every current holder of the slice, this node included; a missing mark counts as 0, and a node that is not a holder cuts nothing.
A lane's last entry is never cut: a spoke's digest reads the tail as an entry.
A scoped cut on a disk node arms a snapshot, so the cut lane reaches disk in one swap with the floor seed that replay starts from.

rules: At each install, a held slice whose holders no longer include this node turns into an orphan, and its per-lane content tails are fixed at that moment.
An orphan is frozen: a new change for it is dropped at the inbound gate and moves no mark, so its floors never rise.
The owner never stamps into an orphan: its own write waits, and a forwarded write is answered 'withheld', until the slice comes back by a latch.
An orphan still answers floor questions with its frozen floors, and still teaches what it holds.
An orphan that the ring gives back to this node stays frozen; it comes back only through a one-teacher latch, even when its floors are equal.
An orphan restored from disk stays frozen even if the restored ring assigns it here.
The boot record lists held and orphan slices apart (a slice mid-latch under its class before the latch), and is rewritten at every mint, fold, abort and shed, before the WAL rows that need it.
On replay, rows of a slice that is neither held nor this life's own lane are not folded, but still move the lane's chain mark.
A spoke is never fed from an orphan's frozen copy, nor from a latch re-entering from one, until the fold.

A slice becomes held only by a one-teacher fold, with three exceptions: the owner's first stamp, a first-ever record reaching its assigned holder, and the arming install.

rules: The teacher ships, lane by lane in ticket order, the slice's entries above the learner's marks, each with its stored pp.
It ships exactly what compaction keeps (the one keep test, with the slice's frontier), never a dropped loser.
It ends with an end marker naming the slice, the view, its own floors as the cut, and the count of records shipped.
The learner aborts the fold if the staged count differs from the count named (a torn copy).
The fold is one step: each copied record goes into its lane at its ticket's place, skipping ones already there, through the cell election.
The learner's floors rise to the teacher's cut, never past it; its applied and shippable marks rise to the cut too.
Then the staged live changes are replayed through the normal ingest; those at or below the cut are dropped.
On a disk node, the folded slice attests nothing (unsealed) until the snapshot swap's echo seals it; the fold arms that swap.

rules: Every scoped change carries pp: the ticket of the previous change this life stamped for the same (lane, slice); the record of last stamps is fed on every scoped commit, epoch 0 included, and never cleared by a shed.
A possession floor rises to a change's ticket only if 0 <= pp <= the floor (the chain rule), at the stamp site, the fast path, the splice and replay; an unknown pp never raises it.
After a splice fills a gap, walk on through later changes of that (lane, slice) whose stored pp now chains, raising the floor; stop at the first gap.
On a scoped node, a change at or below the possession floor is a duplicate and is dropped.
The durable floor rises only on the disk echo of a batch that covers those exact changes, capped at the possession floor, and never for a slice with a splice not yet on disk.
A splice never goes into the WAL as a row; it reaches disk only with the next snapshot swap.
The boot record keeps a floor seed per (lane, slice); replay raises floors from the seed only through chain-checked rows, and slices with an unsaved splice stay at 0.
The first armed install of a life born at epoch 0 raises each floor to its lane tail once (epoch 0 was full broadcast); a restored life never does.
A holder tells its co-holders its floors and durable floors on change, at install, on admit and drain, and in a rotating sweep; a disk node with an unsealed slice tells nothing for it.
A peer's told floors only ever rise within one view; all marks clear at each install, and are voided for a reborn peer, for a slice the peer released, and on a 'none' answer.
Floor messages from another view are dropped.

rules: A view changes only by a ballot that a majority of the old view and a majority of the new view both grant; a voter counts only in the sets it is in.
A node grants a ballot only if its epoch is above the node's committed view.
A node grants at most one ballot per epoch: only if its vote for that epoch is unspent, or was spent on the same proposer.
A ballot names the view it is over; a ballot over a view older than the voter's is refused.
The proposer counts only grants that echo its ballot's epoch and member list; a voter is known by its link's proven id, never by a field in the frame.
Proposing spends the proposer's own vote; it cannot propose at an epoch whose vote it gave to another proposer.
A new ballot's epoch is above the view, above every epoch known to be burned (learned from refusals), and never below the node's own last ballot (V4-25).
A vote is on disk before the VOTE frame leaves, and a self-vote before the PROPOSE leaves; a restart restores the spent vote.
An installed view is on disk the moment it installs.
A node installs a view only with a higher epoch than its own; a client follows its feeder's view even at an equal or lower epoch (I-23).
No ballot outlives an install; a ballot is also dropped when it ages out.
An open ballot is offered again to members that have not voted, so a lost vote heals.
Only the lowest live member proposes; a join that lands elsewhere is passed on one hop to it.
Views spread by flood: every install is announced on every link, every admit announces the view, and a node with a newer view answers a lower one.
Writes commit only while the gate is open: the node is a member of its committed view and a majority of the view is linked (open genesis: always open).
Seeing any epoch above its view closes the gate and starts a view pull; after the pull bound, the gate reopens with an alarm.
A restored node is read-only until a live peer confirms a view at or above its restored one; if nobody does, the lowest restored member ballots the restored view at the next epoch.
A client never proposes, votes or announces a view; membership frames from a client link are dropped.
A client moves off a feeder whose gate is shut to a linked server whose gate is open (V4-58).
A member unlinked for some ticks is a suspect; the lowest live member proposes the view without its dead suspects, only while the live members are a majority.
A suspect whose redial chain is still running is not evicted yet; a suspect that comes back cancels the eviction ballot.
A member proposes taking back a joiner only over a live link to it; an evicted node asks the lowest linked member of its view to propose it back.
Genesis: the lowest id proposes the first view only once it is linked to every host it was given, except one that answered for another resource.
A leaving member asks for the view without itself and the lowest live member proposes it; a leaver may grant its own exit even while epoch-stale.
A leaver whose leave is over never grants a ballot that puts it back in, and never knocks to rejoin.
The leaver goes once a view without it, at or above its epoch, arrives; a member that gets a knock from a non-member answers with its view.
The knock window: a leaver's tick counts toward its bound only while no member that could answer is linked, up to a whole-window cap.

A leave ballot also drops dead suspects when its live members cannot carry it, only while the live members are a majority of the view; a dropped member stays dropped, and a give-up seen once is remembered (V4-60).
A scoped leaver holds its exit until every slice it held is drained to the new holders (the shed bar), bounded by a tick count.
A vote above my view, given to another proposer, not disowned, for a view two or more members apart from mine, holds me (V4-55).
A held node's gate is closed.
A stayer does not count a linked member whose last word names a hold above the stayer's view.
A held node grants only a ballot joint over its held views, or the same proposer's at the same epoch, or one whose members are the held view.
A ballot commits only with a majority of every held view it is joint over too: the proposer's own holds, those its linked members announced, and those named in refusals.
A held node announces its holds: in its hello message, every tick while held, at every change, and once more when the last hold ends; a fresh link's word replaces the old one.
A proposer disowns a hold it has no matching ballot for; the vote stays spent but holds no more, and that is saved to disk.
When holds keep a view stuck and every member is linked, the lowest live member ballots the same members at the next epoch, joint over the holds, only when it can commit.

rules: The ring is built only from the committed view's members, so every node with that view computes the same owners.
Equal hash points are ordered by (point, member, vnode), the same way on every node.
The hash is part of the wire contract: a server's hello message names it, and a member with another ring is refused at the door (V4-14).
A slice's owner is the member at the first ring point at or after the slice's hash, wrapping around.
A slice's holders are the first r distinct members walking on from there; the owner is always the first holder.
Whenever the ring trails the committed view, it is rebuilt before any lookup.
At the flush point, the issuer looks up each waiting write's owner on the current ring: it commits a write it owns and forwards the rest to their owners.
A write's attempt epoch is set again only there (or at the relay when a client's write arrives), never while it waits.
The owner commits a forwarded write only if its attempt epoch equals the owner's committed view, and the view is not open genesis; else 'stale-epoch'.
The owner commits it only if the ring at that view names it the owner; else 'not-owner'.
The owner commits it only if its write gate is open; else 'withheld'.
The owner sends a change only to the slice's holders (and its client links); other members get it only from a teacher.
A change for a slice that this node neither holds nor is assigned is dropped at the inbound gate and moves no mark.

rules: A server announces each resource it holds a copy of: the project, the resource's name and its own address.
A server also announces itself as a machine, with its room and the code it can run, so a leader can find a machine for a new copy.
A server announces everything again on every new link to a directory, so a fresh host rebuilds the whole table from announcements alone.
An entry lives only while its announcer's link to that directory lives: a closed link, or one silent for 20 of the host's beats, drops every entry it made.
A server takes back an entry as soon as it stops holding that copy, because its link stays up for its other resources.
When a machine's directory host stops, the other servers there try to host it after a short random delay, until one does or a link is back.
Across machines, a server announces to every seed directory, so whichever seed a client asks knows every copy.
A client keeps an address only if the HELLO there names the same project and resource; any other answer drops it, and the client tries the next.
A client asks the directory only for a first address; from then on it learns members, slot table and leaders from the resource itself.
A lookup that fails or finds nothing is asked again after a growing delay; it is never given up.
A later announcement of the same entry takes it over, and only the entry's current announcer may take it back, so an old link's death cannot drop a newer entry.
A server that announces is marked seen at once, so a server that leaves cleanly does not leave its dead address behind (v4's I-34).

It is counted because its rules carry stated properties: a client never takes another project's or resource's copy for its own (rule 8, safety); a client can find a live copy while one exists (rules 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 10, liveness); connected clients keep working while the directory is down (rule 9, V5-3); healing can find a machine for a new copy (rule 2). Rules 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 exist in v4 today and would be ported; rules 2, 7 and 9 are new and reasoned from V5-3. rules: W1, intent: the saga library starts a unit's steps only once its intent row is committed, never on an early answer.
W1, step: it sends each next step, the undo decision, each undo and the end only once the write before is committed.
W1, check: a holder that carries on or resolves another unit acts only on committed reads of that unit's intent and lock rows.
W1, claim: a protected write is sent only once its lock claim is committed.
Y: a writer's read waits until its last early-answered write is committed and visible, or known lost.
A follower sends its memory report for a batch only after it has handed the batch to the operating system.
The leader counts its own copy toward replicated only after its own write call for that batch.
The leader's replicated mark is the highest entry a majority holds in memory, and a replicated answer comes only from that mark.
Commit never reads the replicated mark: it moves only on disk reports.
A received answer comes only after the leader has appended the write, never on arrival.
The client keeps an early-answered write pending until it commits, and sends it again after a failover.
Only plain writes may take an early stage; a call that returns a value or a decision answers at commit only.

Member verbs are taken only on links that passed the door; admin asks also need the admin key.

Each server shows its own certificate, signed by the project's CA, and a peer checks it at every handshake.

A client checks a server's certificate against the CA fingerprint in its own credential.

cluster-credentials@per-resource.notes: An open choice the owner has not made: with no #meta and a directory that keeps no log, the project has no replicated place for its CA. This record takes the simplest home: the CA key, single-use join tokens, signing certificates, writing revocations, and dropping an old secret only after every server holds the new one become the operator's or fero deploy's platform's (owner outside); fero keeps the checks. That removes 3 of the study's 12 rules from fero (the CA envelopes to #meta voters, the join token spent by a #meta entry, and 'drop the old secret only after every member holds the next') and keeps the certificate check and the revocation check at the handshake. High 12: keep the PKI inside fero, with envelopes, tokens and revocations as records in each resource's home log (the study's 12 rules). Low 6: rules 1 to 6 only, with certificates left to node:tls's own checks (node:tls is a library and is not counted). CHECKED: 9 -> 12 with owner_split fero 9, outside 3 (skeptic F4). The three PKI rules move to the operator or the platform but are still rules a builder must get right, and the measure counts outside rules (as BUY's JetStream rules). High 12 is the same 12 kept inside fero.

rules: A writer numbers its writes to each partition in the order it sends them.
A group applies a writer's write only if it carries the next number for that partition.
A write that skips a number is refused gap, and the writer sends again, in order, from the first lost one.

rules: A viewer merges the resources' logs by writer time, keeping each resource's own log order, with ties broken by resource name and then position.
A derived record is placed after the source record whose position it carries, whatever their times say.
timeline-merge.rows_note: Not in the base list: V5-4 adds no state. Every row without a timestamp oracle needs the same viewer rules for the same view.
timeline-merge.notes: Recorded so a calibrator can see it, not to be summed: V5-4 stamps nothing new (writer-time already stamps every batch) and keeps no state, so by MECHANISMS section 1 it is not a mechanism, like E-23's merger (low 0). If viewer rules are priced, add these 2 to every row that offers a whole-project view without an oracle. High 3 adds the optional local rule: a derived writer stamps no earlier than its source's time.

rules: On a drain, the controller moves leadership off every group the drained member leads (a transfer command to each group's leader), and never names a draining member as a preferred leader.
A lead hint sets the group's preferred leader in the controller's own records, so the controller's balancing does not hand leadership back.

Who leads what. Each resource has a home group, made at its genesis, whose log holds the settings record, the slot table and the group records (V5-2 (2)). The home group's leader decides the resource's slot moves (move-policy, one decider per resource, so no move lease is needed). Each group's own leader heals that group's copies. Reason: if the home leader healed other groups, decider and executor would be apart, which is cent-co inside a resource and costs E-16's 4 more rules (epoch check, two re-checks, a timeout). Source: E-16 section 4; V5-2 (3).

planner-hints: kept as planner-hints@per-resource (5, the study's planner-hints' same 5 rules after the skeptic check dropped the admin-key rule from both and #meta's lease row from the study's). A leader that heals its own group and a home leader that moves its own slots need no planner (E-16: self heals with no planner; SPACE's self needs none, self+p adds it). But DEP-17 is a MUST (the platform's drains, retirements, gone reports and placement hints), and with no controller those hints can only land at the leaders (RM-05, as for CELL and COMP). The #meta lease row goes; a drain and a retire are the process's own restart and leave. Source: E-16; REQUIREMENTS DEP-17; RM-05; DESIGN-V5 4.2.
